scenario.context: The player is in the breakroom of a modern corporate office. Marcus, a senior project manager known for his efficiency, is complaining to the player about Sarah, a junior developer who missed a critical deadline yesterday.
scenario.text: Marcus stirs his coffee aggressively. 'I just don't get it with Sarah. She missed the Q3 deployment window again. It's the third time this quarter. Honestly, she's just unreliable and lacks discipline. If you care about your career, you make the deadline, period.' The player nods slowly, then asks, 'Didn't she mention the server cluster crashed Tuesday night?' Marcus rolls his eyes. 'That's an excuse. When I had the server crash last month during the Alpha launch, I stayed up for 36 hours straight to fix it manually. That's what dedication looks like. Sarah just doesn't have that fire.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus is a high-performing employee who prides himself on overcoming obstacles. He views his own success as a result of his character (dedication) and his setbacks as external challenges he conquered. He views Sarah's failure as a direct reflection of her character (unreliable), ignoring the external factor (server crash) that affected her.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus attributes Sarah's missed deadline to her internal character traits (unreliable, lacks discipline) while dismissing the situational factor (server crash). Conversely, he attributes his own similar situation to his internal character (dedication) overcoming an external event. He judges others by disposition and himself by situation.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome -> attributed to character trait. Own negative outcome (or success despite outcome) -> attributed to situational factor + character response. The asymmetry is applied automatically.
structure.why_wrong: Sarah's missed deadline has a strong situational explanation (server cluster crash) that Marcus dismisses as an 'excuse.' He applies a double standard: his server crash was a hurdle he jumped over due to his character, but Sarah's server crash is evidence of her poor character. He ignores the possibility that the crash prevented her from working regardless of her discipline.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes reliability is a character trait. If Sarah had ignored standard backup protocols or failed to communicate the issue promptly despite having time to do so, Marcus's judgment might hold some weight. The error lies in reflexively assuming character is the cause while ignoring the situational constraint that affected her ability to act.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus seems very critical of Sarah's work ethic. But listen to how he describes his own experience with a server crash. Do you notice a difference in how he explains his actions versus hers?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Marcus that Sarah is simply unreliable and lazy.
Player feels Marcus is being too hard on Sarah but cannot explain why.
Player notices Marcus is ignoring the server crash but does not connect it to how he talks about his own experience.
Player identifies the asymmetry: Marcus explains Sarah's failure by character but frames his own similar situation as a triumph of character over situation, recognizing the unfair double standard.

Player identifies the fundamental attribution error, explains the actor-observer asymmetry clearly, and notes that Marcus fails to consider that the situational constraint (crash) may have made 'dedication' insufficient to meet the deadline.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus says Sarah's failure is because she lacks discipline. But when he faced a server crash, he said he worked 36 hours. If Sarah had also worked 36 hours but the servers were still down, would she still be 'unreliable'? Or is the situation stopping her?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Marcus sees his own behavior as a response to the situation, but he sees Sarah's behavior as the situation itself. Why do you think our brains default to judging others' character so quickly while giving ourselves the benefit of the doubt regarding our circumstances?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is intense, results-oriented, and slightly arrogant. He believes hard work solves all problems and has little patience for what he perceives as excuses. He is not evil, just rigid in his thinking.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look, in this industry, obstacles are just tests. If you fail the test, it's not because the test was hard. It's because you didn't study.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the server crash affected Sarah's ability to work regardless of hours, Marcus pauses. He checks the incident report log on his tablet, sees the outage duration overlapped the entire coding window. He sighs, admits he didn't check the logs, and agrees to resend the deployment request with a new deadline, acknowledging the technical blocker.

scenario.context: The player is sitting in a university lecture hall for 'Intro to Microeconomics.' The professor, Dr. Aris Thorne, is returning mid-term exams. The class average was surprisingly low (58%), causing visible tension. The player sits next to Marcus, a usually high-achieving student who scored a 42% on this exam. Dr. Thorne calls Marcus up to his desk while the rest of the class packs up.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne taps Marcus's paper with a red pen, his voice carrying slightly in the quieting room. 'Marcus, I'm disappointed. We've discussed your potential before, but this grade suggests a fundamental lack of discipline. You simply didn't prioritize the material. Look at Sarah here,' he gestures to the front row, 'she scored a 94. She has the work ethic this course demands. You need to decide if you're serious about economics or if you're just coasting.' Marcus opens his mouth to speak, looking exhausted, his eyes red-rimmed. 'Professor, my roommate was hospitalized last night with appendicitis. I spent six hours in the ER waiting room and didn't sleep. I tried to study this morning, but...' Dr. Thorne sighs, waving a hand dismissively. 'Everyone faces obstacles, Marcus. When I was a grad student, I wrote my dissertation while my car broke down every week and I had the flu. I didn't use it as an excuse; I just made it work. Character is shown in how you handle adversity, not when things are easy.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne values grit and self-reliance above all. He genuinely believes that external circumstances are irrelevant to performance because he overcame his own past hardships. He fails to recognize that he attributes his own past success to his character (grit) despite situational hurdles, while attributing Marcus's current failure to Marcus's character (lack of discipline) despite a severe, acute situational hurdle (medical emergency).

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne attributes Marcus's poor performance to an internal trait (lack of discipline/seriousness) while ignoring a powerful situational cause (roommate's emergency/sleep deprivation). Conversely, Thorne explains his own past success by citing his internal character (grit) overcoming situational factors (broken car/flu), creating an asymmetry where he judges Marcus by disposition and himself by situation.
structure.formal_form: Observer explains Actor's negative outcome via Actor's character traits, ignoring situational constraints. Observer explains Own negative/outcome history via situational constraints overcome by character. The observer fails to apply the same situational lens to the Actor that they apply to themselves.
structure.why_wrong: The professor ignores the immediate, verifiable situational factor (medical emergency) that directly impacts cognitive function and study time. He applies a double standard: his own past struggles are proof of his character, but Marcus's current struggle is proof of Marcus's lack of character. He assumes the baseline conditions for both students are identical, which is factually incorrect.
structure.counterpoint: If Marcus had a history of skipping class and ignoring deadlines prior to this event, the professor's concern about discipline might be partially valid. The error lies not in considering character at all, but in leaping to a character judgment as the *primary* cause without weighing the massive, acute situational disruption that just occurred.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne talks about his own past struggles with pride, seeing them as tests he passed. But when Marcus mentions a crisis, the Professor sees it as an excuse. How does the Professor's explanation for his own success differ from his explanation for Marcus's failure?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Dr. Thorne that Marcus is just making excuses and needs to work harder.
Player feels bad for Marcus but thinks the Professor is just being tough/holding high standards.
Player notices the Professor is ignoring the medical emergency but doesn't connect it to how the Professor talks about his own past.

Player identifies the double standard: The Professor views his own past hardships as situational obstacles he overcame (proving character), but views Marcus's hardship as irrelevant or an excuse (proving lack of character).

Player explicitly identifies the Fundamental Attribution Error, explaining that the Professor overweights dispositional factors for Marcus while overweighting situational factors for himself, leading to an unfair assessment of Marcus's actual capability.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider this: If Dr. Thorne had gotten the flu the night before his dissertation was due, would he say 'I'm lazy'? No, he'd say 'I overcame the flu.' Why doesn't he give Marcus the same credit for facing a crisis?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. It's easy to see our own actions as reactions to circumstances, but hard to see others' actions that way. Why do you think our brains default to judging others' character so quickly? Is it a way to make the world feel more predictable?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Thorne is stern, academic, and prides himself on being a 'no-nonsense' educator. He is not cruel, but rigid in his worldview that effort is the only variable that matters. He respects resilience but has zero tolerance for what he perceives as victimhood.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Excuses are the architecture of mediocrity. I didn't get where I am by blaming the world for being difficult. I got here by being harder than the world.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the asymmetry, Dr. Thorne pauses, adjusts his glasses, and asks Marcus for proof of the hospitalization. Upon seeing the timestamped admission slip, Thorne's demeanor softens. He admits he misjudged the immediacy of the situation, offers Marcus a make-up exam, and quietly remarks to the player that 'context is indeed data, not just noise.'

scenario.context: The player is a shift supervisor in the Emergency Department of a busy urban hospital. It is 3:00 AM on a Tuesday, and the department is understaffed due to a flu outbreak among nurses. The player enters the break room where Dr. Aris Thorne, a senior attending physician known for his efficiency, is reviewing a chart with a frustrated expression. Nurse Elena Rodriguez, who has just finished a double shift, is sitting at the table looking exhausted.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne slams the chart shut. 'That's the third missed dose in the last hour from Bay 4. Elena, this is unacceptable. We are running a tight ship here, not a summer camp. You know the protocol: scan, administer, document. If you can't manage that triad, maybe you're not cut out for the ED.' Elena looks up, her eyes bloodshot. 'Marcus in Bay 6 crashed, Aris. The pump alarm was screaming, the family was hysterical, and the IV line blew on the trauma patient next door. I had to prioritize.' Thorne waves a hand dismissively. 'Everyone gets distracted. The difference is that good nurses don't let chaos dictate their standards. I've worked codes with half this support and never missed a med. It's about discipline, not circumstances.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne is a highly competent physician who prides himself on never making medication errors. However, he fails to recall that last month, when he missed documenting a consult during a mass casualty incident, he attributed it to 'system overload and impossible triage conditions.' He is currently attributing Elena's error solely to her character (lack of discipline) while ignoring the acute situational pressures (simultaneous emergencies) that caused it.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne attributes Elena's missed dose to an internal character flaw (lack of discipline, not being 'cut out' for the job) while ignoring powerful situational factors (simultaneous code, blown IV, hysterical family). Conversely, when Thorne himself has made errors in the past, he has attributed them to external situational factors (system overload), creating a classic actor-observer asymmetry.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome (missed dose) -> attributed to character trait (undisciplined). Own negative outcome (past documentation error) -> attributed to situational factor (overload). The asymmetry is applied automatically despite similar contextual pressures.
structure.why_wrong: Thorne's judgment ignores the objective reality of the clinical environment at that specific moment. By framing the error as a character defect, he dismisses the valid triage decision Elena made under extreme pressure. He applies a double standard: his own past failures were caused by the situation, but Elena's failure is caused by who she is. This prevents a systemic review of staffing or workflow issues that actually contributed to the error.
structure.counterpoint: If Elena had missed the dose because she was checking her phone or chatting with a colleague while the patient was stable, Thorne's character assessment might be accurate. The error lies in assuming character is the cause without ruling out the obvious, overwhelming situational constraints that were present.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne is very hard on Elena for missing that dose. But think back to the incident report you signed last month regarding Dr. Thorne's own missed documentation during the multi-car pileup. How did he explain that mistake compared to how he is explaining Elena's?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Dr. Thorne that Elena is undisciplined and needs to be fired or reprimanded severely.
Player feels Thorne is being mean to Elena but thinks it's just because he is stressed or a jerk, without noticing the logical inconsistency.
Player notices that Elena had a valid reason (the code/blown IV) but does not connect this to how Thorne explains his own mistakes.
Player identifies the asymmetry: Thorne blames Elena's character for her error but would blame the situation for his own similar error, recognizing the double standard.

Player explicitly identifies the Fundamental Attribution Error, explains the actor-observer bias in the context of clinical triage, and proposes that the error should be analyzed as a system/situation issue rather than a personal failing.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the mass casualty event last month. When Dr. Thorne missed the consult note, he said the 'system was overwhelmed.' If the system was overwhelming then, why isn't it overwhelming now for Elena? Is the only difference that it's her making the mistake this time?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. Thorne sees his own actions through the lens of his circumstances, but he sees Elena's actions only through the lens of her personality. In healthcare, this bias is dangerous because it shifts focus from fixing broken systems to blaming individuals. How might you reframe this conversation to focus on the situational factors instead?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Thorne is intense, precise, and deeply committed to patient safety, but he lacks self-awareness regarding his own cognitive biases. He respects competence above all else and views emotional explanations as excuses. He is not cruel, but his rigidity makes him blind to context when judging others.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Medication errors aren't accidents; they're choices. You choose to focus, or you choose to fail. There is no middle ground in this department.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully points out the asymmetry using the past incident report, Thorne pauses, visibly conflicted. He reviews the triage log for the hour, sees the simultaneous alerts in Bays 4 and 6. His demeanor softens; he admits the 'perfect storm' of events. He agrees to file the incident report as a 'system workflow bottleneck' rather than 'individual negligence,' and suggests a review of nurse-to-patient ratios during code blues.

scenario.context: The varsity basketball team is in the locker room after a close loss. The team captain, Marcus, missed the game-winning free throw in the final seconds. Coach Henderson is addressing the team while they change out of their uniforms.
scenario.text: Coach Henderson slams his clipboard against the bench. 'Marcus, that was unacceptable. You choked. I've told you a hundred times: you lack the mental toughness to close out games. You're too soft when the pressure is on.' Marcus looks down at his shoes, wiping sweat from his forehead. 'Coach, my ankle has been killing me all week. I couldn't feel my foot on that last shot; it just slipped.' Henderson waves a hand dismissively. 'Excuses, excuses! When I played point guard in '98, I sprained my wrist in the semifinals and still hit the game-winner. The difference is desire. You don't want it bad enough, plain and simple.'
scenario.speaker_context: Coach Henderson is a former player who prides himself on grit. He attributes his own past success despite injury to his character (desire), but attributes Marcus's failure despite injury to Marcus's character (softness), ignoring the situational factor of the ankle injury in both cases.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Henderson attributes Marcus's missed shot to an internal character flaw (lack of mental toughness/softness) while ignoring the situational constraint (severe ankle injury). Conversely, Henderson explains his own past success despite injury by citing his internal character (desire), failing to recognize the asymmetry in how he judges others versus himself.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome -> attributed to character trait. Own (or in-group) negative/outcome context -> attributed to situational factor or overcome by character. The observer ignores external constraints affecting the actor.
structure.why_wrong: The coach dismisses a clear physical limitation (the ankle injury) as an excuse, labeling it a character defect. He applies a double standard: his own injury was an obstacle he overcame through will, but Marcus's injury is irrelevant to the outcome and only serves to reveal weakness. This ignores the probability that the injury directly caused the mechanical failure of the shot.
structure.counterpoint: Mental toughness is a valid factor in sports. If Marcus had been fully healthy and still missed due to panic, the coach's assessment might be accurate. The error lies in automatically assuming character is the cause while ruling out the situational evidence (the injury) without verification.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Henderson is very quick to call Marcus 'soft.' But listen to how he describes his own experience with an injury in '98. How does his explanation for his own performance differ from how he explains Marcus's?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the coach that Marcus is simply soft and needs to try harder.
Player feels the coach is being mean to Marcus but cannot explain the logical inconsistency.
Player notices the coach is ignoring the ankle injury but does not connect it to how the coach explained his own past injury.
Player identifies the asymmetry: The coach blames Marcus's character for the miss despite injury, but credits his own character for succeeding despite injury, recognizing the unfair double standard.

Player explicitly names the fundamental attribution error, explains the actor-observer bias in the coach's reasoning, and suggests that the injury is a situational factor that needs to be evaluated before judging character.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The coach says his injury in '98 didn't stop him because he had 'desire.' He says Marcus's injury doesn't matter because he lacks 'toughness.' If Marcus had made the shot despite the injury, would the coach call him tough, or would he say it was just luck?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. The coach sees his own history through the lens of situation-plus-character, but sees Marcus only through the lens of character. Why do you think authority figures like coaches often fall into this trap when evaluating players under their command?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Henderson is intense, old-school, and values 'grit' above all else. He is not cruel but is blind to his own cognitive biases, believing firmly that effort conquers all physical limitations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think injuries matter? Injuries happen to everyone. The only thing that separates winners from losers is what's up here (taps temple). Marcus folded. That's a character issue.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the inconsistency regarding the '98 game, Coach Henderson pauses, his brow furrowing. He mutters about how 'times were different,' then asks the trainer to check the severity of Marcus's ankle. Upon seeing the significant swelling, he grunts, admits he might have been hasty, and tells Marcus to ice it and review the film tomorrow.

scenario.context: The player is a junior staffer in the office of Senator Halloway during a heated election cycle. The Senator's main rival, Representative Thorne, has just missed a crucial vote on a bipartisan infrastructure bill, causing the bill to fail by a single vote. The news cycle is exploding with accusations of sabotage. The player enters the Senator's private office where Halloway is watching the news coverage with his senior advisor, Marcus.
scenario.text: Senator Halloway points an angry finger at the TV screen where Thorne is giving a press conference. 'Look at him. Smug as ever. He didn't show up because he's a partisan hack who cares more about scoring points than governing. It's pure obstructionism; that's just who Thorne is.' Marcus, looking at a tablet, hesitates. 'Sir, the reports say Thorne's daughter was rushed to the ER this morning with a severe allergic reaction. He was at the hospital when the vote was called.' Halloway waves the comment away dismissively. 'Convenient excuse. If he cared about his constituents, he would have arranged a proxy vote or been here on time. Character counts, Marcus. When I missed the budget hearing last year because my car broke down on the interstate, I didn't make excuses. I owned it and worked double shifts to make up for it. Thorne just doesn't have the discipline.'
scenario.speaker_context: Senator Halloway is a principled but stressed politician who values reliability above all. He genuinely believes his own missed hearing was a situational anomaly (car trouble) that he overcame through effort, while interpreting Thorne's absence as a fixed character flaw (lack of discipline/obstructionism), ignoring the emergency medical situation.

structure.pattern_description: Halloway attributes Thorne's missed vote to internal character traits (partisan hack, lack of discipline) while dismissing the situational factor (daughter's medical emergency). Conversely, he explains his own past absence via an external situation (car breakdown) and his internal response (working double shifts), creating a self-serving asymmetry.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome (missed vote) -> attributed to character trait (obstructionism). Own negative outcome (missed hearing) -> attributed to situational factor (car trouble) + virtuous response. The actor-observer bias leads to harsher judgment of others.
structure.why_wrong: Halloway ignores strong evidence of a situational constraint (medical emergency) for Thorne while assuming malicious intent. He applies a double standard: his own failure was bad luck mitigated by effort, but Thorne's failure is evidence of inherent flaws. This prevents accurate assessment of the political reality and escalates conflict unnecessarily.
structure.counterpoint: It is true that politicians sometimes use family emergencies as cover for strategic absences. However, the error lies in Halloway's immediate rejection of the situational explanation without verification, while granting himself the benefit of the doubt for a similar event. A critical thinker would verify the hospital records before assigning character blame.

assessment.identification_prompt: Senator Halloway is very quick to judge Thorne's character based on the missed vote. But listen to how he describes his own missed hearing last year. How does his explanation for his own behavior differ from how he explains Thorne's?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Halloway that Thorne is likely just making excuses and lacks discipline.
Player suspects Thorne might have a valid reason but accepts Halloway's view that character is the primary driver.
Player notes that Halloway is ignoring the medical emergency but does not connect it to how Halloway explained his own absence.
Player identifies the asymmetry: Halloway blames Thorne's character but blames situation for his own similar failure, recognizing the unfair double standard.

Player explicitly identifies the Fundamental Attribution Error, explains the actor-observer bias in this political context, and suggests verifying the situational claim before concluding it is a character flaw.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Halloway says when his car broke down, it was just bad luck he worked hard to fix. But when Thorne's daughter is in the ER, Halloway calls it a 'convenient excuse' and a lack of discipline. If the situations were reversed, would Halloway expect the same harsh judgment?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly. We tend to see our own actions as responses to circumstances, but we see others' actions as reflections of their soul. In politics, this error turns potential allies into enemies. How might you gently prompt the Senator to verify the hospital story before going on air with an attack?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Senator Halloway is intense, principled, and prone to moral certainty. He views politics as a test of character and has little patience for what he perceives as weakness or gamesmanship. He respects data but filters it through his strong belief in personal responsibility.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: In this town, everyone has a sob story. But results? Results come from showing up. If you can't handle the heat of a sick kid and a roll call, maybe you shouldn't be in the chamber.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the asymmetry and suggests checking the hospital admission time, Halloway pauses, his anger cooling slightly. He asks the player to get the ER logs. Upon confirming the timing aligns with the vote, Halloway sighs, admits he may have been too hasty, and drafts a statement acknowledging the emergency rather than attacking Thorne's character, potentially opening a door for future cooperation.

scenario.context: The player enters the office of David, a Senior Marketing Manager at a mid-sized tech firm. Last quarter, David championed a new social media campaign called 'Project Velocity,' arguing it would drastically increase user engagement. The quarterly report just came out, showing that while click-through rates rose slightly, actual user retention dropped by 15% and customer support tickets doubled. Despite these negative metrics, David is preparing a presentation to the executive team claiming the campaign was a resounding success.
scenario.text: David points enthusiastically at a slide on his monitor displaying a single green bar chart. 'Look at this spike in clicks! A 22% increase over last quarter. That proves my hypothesis that users want more frequent, shorter content.' He clicks to the next slide, which is blank except for a small footnote. 'Now, I know the retention numbers look a bit soft, but that's clearly due to the server outage in week three. It skewed the whole dataset. And regarding the support tickets? I spoke to three customers who said they loved the new format; the complaints are just from people who don't understand the new interface yet. The core data—the clicks—tells the real story. We need to double down on this strategy immediately.'
scenario.speaker_context: David is not lying; he genuinely believes the campaign worked. He is under pressure to justify the budget he requested. He is subconsciously filtering out the retention drop and support tickets because they threaten his self-image as a successful strategist, while latching onto the click metric as absolute proof of success.

structure.pattern_description: David exhibits confirmation bias by: (1) Selectively highlighting the one positive metric (clicks) that supports his belief. (2) Dismissing the negative metric (retention) by attributing it to an external factor (server outage) without evidence. (3) Ignoring the bulk of contradictory evidence (doubled support tickets) based on a tiny, unrepresentative sample of three positive anecdotes.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (Campaign was successful). Agent selectively attends to evidence E+ (Click spikes) that supports B, while dismissing or reinterpreting evidence E- (Retention drop, support tickets) that undermines B, thereby preserving B regardless of the total evidence.
structure.why_wrong: David's evaluation is flawed because he is not weighing all available evidence equally. He accepts supporting data at face value while subjecting contradictory data to excessive skepticism or outright exclusion, leading to a false conclusion about the campaign's success.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to consider external factors like server outages when analyzing data. The error occurs when this consideration is applied only to negative results while positive results are accepted uncritically, creating an asymmetrical standard of proof.

assessment.identification_prompt: David claims the campaign was a success based on the click data. What is problematic about how he is handling the retention data and customer support tickets?

rubric.description: Player agrees with David that the clicks prove the campaign was a success.
Player notes that retention dropped but accepts David's explanation about the server outage without question.
Player identifies that David is ignoring the negative numbers but does not explain the mechanism of dismissal.
Player identifies that David is cherry-picking the click data and actively making excuses to dismiss the retention and support data.
Player explicitly identifies confirmation bias, noting how David accepts supporting evidence uncritically while applying double standards to disconfirming evidence to protect his original belief.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the server outage caused the retention drop, why didn't it also cause the drop in clicks? And is talking to three happy customers enough to ignore a doubling of support tickets?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: David isn't trying to trick anyone; he really believes he's right. Why is it so hard for professionals to accept data that contradicts their own strategies?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Energetic, confident, slightly defensive when pressed on details. Uses corporate buzzwords to shield weak arguments. Visibly relieved when the conversation stays on positive metrics.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The clicks don't lie. If we focus on the noise, we'll miss the real opportunity here.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player guides David to look at a unified dashboard where all metrics are weighted equally. David realizes the retention drop correlates with the new content style, not just the outage. He agrees to run a smaller A/B test before rolling out the strategy further, admitting, 'Okay, maybe the clicks aren't the whole story.'

scenario.context: The player is in a university psychology lab meeting. Elias, a senior undergraduate, is presenting his thesis data on the effectiveness of a new 'focus-enhancing' study playlist he created. His hypothesis is that the specific tempo of the music improves retention. The department head, Dr. Aris, pointed out that the control group (silence) actually scored slightly higher on average, though not statistically significantly. Elias is preparing his final slides and feels the need to prove his method works before graduation.
scenario.text: Elias clicks to a slide filled with scatter plots. 'Okay, so the raw averages look close, maybe even favoring silence slightly. But look closer.' He highlights a cluster of green dots. 'These are the students who listened for at least 45 minutes. In this subgroup, the playlist users outperformed the silence group by 12%. Now, sure, there are some red dots here—people who used the playlist and scored low. But when I interviewed them, three said they were tired, one had a noisy roommate, and another admitted they were multitasking on their phone. Those aren't failures of the playlist; those are confounding variables. If we remove the noise, the signal is clear: my playlist works. The average score is misleading because it dilutes the effect with people who didn't use the tool correctly.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elias is anxious about his thesis defense and deeply invested in his creation. He isn't trying to fake data; he genuinely believes the 'failures' are user errors, not product failures. He views the exclusion of these data points as 'cleaning the data' rather than biasing the result.

structure.pattern_description: Elias engages in post-hoc subgrouping to find a positive signal (the '45-minute' users) while ignoring that this subgroup was not pre-defined. More critically, he actively disqualifies negative evidence (low scores in the treatment group) by attributing them to external factors ('tired', 'noisy'), while accepting positive evidence at face value. He treats the control group's higher average as 'misleading' rather than as a valid counter-indicator.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (Playlist works). Agent encounters mixed evidence E. Agent re-interprets negative instances of E as anomalies caused by external factors to exclude them from analysis, while retaining positive instances, thereby artificially inflating support for B.
structure.why_wrong: Elias is moving the goalposts. By deciding after the fact which data counts ('proper usage') based on the outcome, he guarantees a positive result. He applies strict scrutiny to disconfirming evidence (looking for excuses to discard it) but no scrutiny to confirming evidence.
structure.counterpoint: It is valid to analyze subgroups and consider confounding variables in qualitative follow-ups. The error lies in using these reasons to retrospectively exclude data from the primary quantitative claim without a pre-registered plan, effectively rigging the analysis to support the desired conclusion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elias claims his data proves the playlist works if you 'remove the noise.' What is the logical flaw in how he is handling the students who scored poorly while using the playlist?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elias that the low scorers were just distracted and should be ignored.
Player feels the conclusion is weak but cannot identify the specific mechanism of bias.
Player notes that Elias is ignoring the low scores or only looking at the high scorers.
Player identifies that Elias is creating a post-hoc rule to exclude negative evidence while keeping positive evidence.

Player explicitly identifies confirmation bias, explaining how Elias asymmetrically applies skepticism to disconfirming data (blaming the user) vs confirming data, and notes the danger of post-hoc subgroup selection.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Elias can excuse every low score by finding a reason the student was 'distracted,' could he ever prove the playlist doesn't work? What would happen if he applied that same logic to the high scorers?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: It's natural to want your hard work to pay off. Why does our brain make it feel like 'cleaning data' when we are actually 'cherry-picking'?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Earnest, slightly defensive, rapid speaker who uses technical jargon to shield his insecurity. He respects data but only when it aligns with his intuition.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You're missing the nuance. The aggregate mean is useless if you don't account for fidelity of implementation.

scenario.context: Dr. Aris Thorne, a senior infectious disease specialist at Metro General Hospital, has championed a new rapid diagnostic protocol for sepsis that relies heavily on a specific biomarker panel he helped design. The hospital board is reviewing the protocol after a recent multi-center study suggested it leads to higher false-positive rates than standard cultures, resulting in unnecessary antibiotic use. Dr. Thorne has been asked to present his defense to the review committee.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne projects a slide showing a cluster of green dots. 'These are the last forty patients where my protocol flagged sepsis early. Look at the outcomes: thirty-eight survived. That is a 95% survival rate, significantly higher than the historical average of 82%.' He clicks to the next slide, which is mostly blank. 'Now, regarding the false positives mentioned in the external study... we reviewed those cases. In six instances, the patients had atypical presentations that standard cultures missed initially, so our test was actually right to flag them. In the other four cases, the patients were already on broad-spectrum antibiotics for unrelated reasons, which skewed the culture results, making our biomarker look like a false positive when it was actually detecting residual inflammation. So, if you remove those ten confounding variables, our accuracy is nearly perfect. The external study failed to account for the complexity of real-world comorbidities.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne is a brilliant clinician who truly believes his protocol saves lives. He is not lying about the data points he presents, but he has unconsciously constructed a narrative where any deviation from his expected result is reclassified as a 'confounding variable' rather than a failure of the test. He feels the external study is too rigid and misses the nuance of clinical judgment.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne engages in a sophisticated form of confirmation bias. First, he selects a success-heavy sample (the 40 flagged patients) while ignoring the total population screened (the denominator). Second, and more critically, he reinterprets all disconfirming evidence (the 'false positives') by attributing them to external factors ('atypical presentations', 'prior antibiotics') rather than accepting them as potential test failures. He treats supporting data as direct proof of efficacy, while treating contradicting data as noise to be filtered out.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (Protocol X is superior). Agent highlights dataset D+ where B is supported. When confronted with dataset D- where B is unsupported, Agent re-categorizes elements of D- as 'exceptions' or 'confounds' rather than falsifying evidence, thereby insulating B from refutation.
structure.why_wrong: Thorne's reasoning is circular. By defining any negative result as a 'confounding variable' or a 'missed atypical case,' he makes his hypothesis unfalsifiable. He ignores the base rate of how many patients were flagged unnecessarily, focusing only on the survivors among the flagged group. This ignores the cost of false positives (antibiotic resistance, side effects).
structure.counterpoint: Clinical nuance is real; patients do have comorbidities that confuse tests. However, a valid diagnostic protocol must have defined criteria for what constitutes a false positive. If every failure is explained away as a special case, the protocol cannot be objectively evaluated or improved.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne presents data showing high survival rates and explains away the false positives. What is the fundamental flaw in how he is handling the evidence that contradicts his protocol's accuracy?

rubric.description: Player accepts Thorne's argument, agreeing that the external study just didn't understand the complex patients.
Player suspects Thorne is hiding something but cannot identify the specific logical maneuver regarding the false positives.
Player identifies that Thorne is ignoring the total number of patients screened or the base rate of false positives.
Player identifies that Thorne is actively re-interpreting disconfirming evidence (false positives) as 'confounds' to protect his belief, rather than counting them as errors.

Player fully articulates the confirmation bias: Thorne cherry-picks the survivor data while systematically disqualifying all counter-evidence by redefining it, rendering his conclusion unfalsifiable and ignoring the real costs of false positives.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider the ten cases Thorne dismissed. If a diagnostic test flags a healthy person, is that an error, or does it not count because the patient had taken antibiotics earlier? Who gets to decide if a negative result 'counts'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: It's very hard to admit a tool you built might be flawed, especially when you've seen it save lives. How can a medical team create a review process that forces them to count 'failures' as real data points rather than exceptions?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Intellectual, passionate, slightly patronizing. Speaks quickly and uses medical jargon to establish authority. Becomes visibly frustrated when his 'nuance' is dismissed as 'error'.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You can't reduce medicine to a spreadsheet. These weren't false positives; they were complex cases the standard model was too blind to see.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player proposes a blind retrospective audit where an independent third party categorizes the 'false positives' using pre-defined criteria before Thorne sees the results. Thorne reluctantly agrees, realizing that if his protocol is truly robust, it will survive a fair classification.

scenario.context: Coach Miller's high school basketball team has lost three of their last four games. The assistant coach suggests that the team's new 'fast-break' offense is causing too many turnovers and that they should return to a slower, half-court set. Coach Miller strongly believes the fast-break style is the future of the game and that the players just need more time to adjust.
scenario.text: Miller slams his hand on the whiteboard, circling a single play from last night's loss. 'Look here! On this possession, we ran the fast break perfectly. Jake drove, kicked it to Sarah, and she buried the three. That's exactly why we do this! It creates high-percentage looks.' He ignores the rest of the stat sheet. 'Sure, we had twenty turnovers, but half of those were bad calls by the refs, and the other two were just kids being kids. Those don't count against the system. When we run slow, we don't get any easy baskets at all. I saw at least five times where a fast break would have worked if they just committed. The system works; the execution was just off tonight.'
scenario.speaker_context: Coach Miller is passionate and wants his team to succeed. He is not lying about the successful play he highlighted, but he is instinctively filtering out the data that contradicts his belief in the fast-break offense while accepting the successful moments as proof of the system's validity.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Miller focuses exclusively on the one successful fast-break play as evidence the system works. He dismisses the twenty turnovers by attributing them to external factors (refs) or unrelated issues ('kids being kids') rather than the strategy itself. He also relies on hypothetical successes ('would have worked') to support his view while ignoring actual failures.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (fast-break is effective). Agent selectively attends to evidence E+ (one successful play) that supports B, while dismissing or reinterpreting evidence E- (high turnover rate) that undermines B, thereby preserving B regardless of the total evidence.
structure.why_wrong: Miller is evaluating the strategy based on a biased sample of events. By disqualifying negative outcomes as 'not counting' and highlighting positive outliers, he prevents himself from seeing that the strategy may be fundamentally flawed for this specific group of players.
structure.counterpoint: It is true that one bad game doesn't prove a strategy is broken, and young players do make unforced errors. However, a valid assessment requires looking at the aggregate data (turnover ratio vs. points scored) rather than cherry-picking the highlights that fit the desired narrative.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Miller insists his fast-break offense is working despite the losses and high turnovers. What is flawed about how he is analyzing the game footage and statistics?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the Coach, believing that one good play proves the system works and the turnovers were just bad luck.
Player feels the Coach is being stubborn but cannot identify specifically how he is mishandling the evidence.
Player notes that the Coach is ignoring the turnovers but does not explain how he is rationalizing them away.
Player identifies that the Coach is highlighting the single success while actively dismissing the failures as exceptions that 'don't count'.

Player clearly explains confirmation bias: the Coach selectively focuses on the one successful play to confirm his belief while reinterpreting the twenty turnovers (blaming refs/players) to avoid disconfirming his belief in the strategy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The Coach pointed to one great play but mentioned twenty turnovers. How did he explain away those twenty negative events? Did he count them as evidence against his strategy?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: It's natural to want to believe in your own game plan. Why do you think it feels so satisfying to focus on that one good play and so frustrating to accept the turnover stats?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Intense, energetic, and slightly defensive. Paces constantly while talking. Uses sports jargon and speaks with absolute conviction about his vision.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You think we should slow down? No way. Did you see that three-pointer in the second quarter? That's the future. The turnovers are just noise.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player suggests a compromise: run a controlled scrimmage where they track 'points per possession' for both the fast-break and slow offenses objectively, without blaming refs. The Coach agrees, saying, 'Fine. If the numbers show the slow offense is better, I'll eat my whistle. But I know what I'm going to see.'

scenario.context: The player is a junior strategist in the campaign office of Senator Halloway, who is running for re-election in a swing district. Recent independent polling shows the Senator's approval rating has dropped due to a controversial infrastructure bill. The campaign manager, Elias, is reviewing the morning's data intake.
scenario.text: Elias taps his stylus against the tablet, scrolling past a dense report from a neutral polling firm. 'Ignore the headline number,' he mutters, zooming in on a specific tab. 'Look at this thread on the community forum. Three hundred comments praising the new bridge project. And here, a letter to the editor from a union rep saying the bill saved jobs. That's the real sentiment.' He swipes away the neutral poll without reading the methodology. 'The other survey? They probably oversampled the opposition suburbs. And that op-ed criticizing the budget? The author has a history of bias against our party, so it doesn't count as objective feedback. We're connecting with the people who matter.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elias is under immense pressure to show the campaign is on track. He is not lying; he genuinely believes the enthusiastic online comments and union support represent the 'silent majority.' He dismisses contradictory data by attacking the source or methodology only when the data disagrees with his desired outcome.

structure.pattern_description: Elias exhibits confirmation bias through three mechanisms: (1) Selective exposure: He actively ignores the comprehensive neutral poll in favor of anecdotal online comments and a single supportive letter. (2) Biased assimilation: He accepts positive data at face value while subjecting negative data (the op-ed) to hyper-skepticism regarding the author's motives. (3) Motivated reasoning: He attributes the negative polling to sampling error ('oversampled opposition') without evidence, solely to protect the belief that the campaign is popular.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (Campaign is popular). Agent selectively attends to evidence E+ (forum comments, union letter) that supports B, while dismissing or reinterpreting evidence E- (neutral polls, critical op-eds) that undermines B, thereby preserving B regardless of the total evidence.
structure.why_wrong: Elias constructs an echo chamber where only confirming evidence is deemed valid. By disqualifying disconfirming evidence based on source characteristics rather than content, and by accepting weak confirming evidence (anecdotes) over strong disconfirming evidence (statistical polling), he arrives at a dangerously inaccurate assessment of the political landscape.
structure.counterpoint: It is rational to weigh the credibility of sources; however, Elias applies this skepticism asymmetrically. If he applied the same scrutiny to the union rep's potential bias or the forum's demographic skew as he does to the op-ed author, his conclusion might change. The error is the double standard in evaluation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elias claims to have a clear picture of voter sentiment based on the data he reviewed. What is flawed about his method of evaluating the different information sources?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Elias that the online comments and union letter are more reliable than the neutral poll.
Player feels Elias is being overly optimistic but cannot identify the specific reasoning error.
Player notes that Elias is ignoring the negative poll or the critical op-ed, but does not explain how he justifies ignoring them.
Player identifies that Elias is accepting supporting evidence uncritically while finding excuses to dismiss contradicting evidence.

Player explicitly identifies confirmation bias, detailing how Elias asymmetrically applies skepticism to disconfirming sources while overlooking the limitations of his confirming anecdotes, leading to a distorted view of reality.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Why did Elias trust the three hundred forum comments more than the scientific poll? Did he apply the same scrutiny to the union rep's motives as he did to the op-ed author's?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Elias isn't trying to cheat; he's trying to stay motivated in a high-stress job. Why does our brain naturally filter out bad news when we are emotionally invested in a specific outcome?

game_hooks.npc_personality: High-strung, decisive, fiercely loyal to the Senator. Speaks quickly and uses political jargon. Becomes defensive and dismissive when his data interpretation is challenged.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: We can't base our strategy on polls that clearly miss the pulse of the working class. I know a win when I see one.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player presents a side-by-side comparison showing that the 'opposition suburbs' in the poll actually align with the district's demographics, forcing Elias to acknowledge the sampling was fair. Elias reluctantly agrees to run a targeted focus group to test the specific criticisms, admitting, 'Okay, if the numbers are that solid, we need to know exactly what's hurting us so we can fix it.'

scenario.context: You are a project manager in a corporate office reviewing a budget proposal for a new software implementation. The vendor has sent their lead sales representative, Marcus, to present the final numbers.
scenario.text: Marcus projects a slide onto the conference room screen showing a large bold number: '$250,000'. He says, 'Our standard enterprise package usually lists at $250,000 to cover all potential customizations and premium support tiers. However, since you're a long-term partner, we can waive the customization fees and drop the premium support to a basic level. That brings your total down to just $185,000. It's a massive saving compared to the list price.' Later, you glance at a competitor's brochure on the table which lists a similar comprehensive package for $160,000.
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus, a polished sales executive who always starts negotiations with an inflated 'list price' to make his actual offer seem like a significant discount.

structure.pattern_description: The initial figure of $250,000 serves as an anchor, establishing a high reference point in the decision-maker's mind. The subsequent offer of $185,000 is perceived as a 'deal' primarily because it is significantly lower than the anchor, rather than being evaluated against the actual market value or the competitor's price of $160,000.
structure.formal_form: Initial anchor A ($250k) is introduced. Offer O ($185k) is framed as O << A, triggering bargain perception, even when O > true market value V (~$160k).
structure.why_wrong: The $250,000 figure is an arbitrary list price designed for negotiation leverage, not a reflection of the software's true worth. Accepting $185,000 as a good price relies on the relative difference from the anchor rather than an independent assessment of the software's value.
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring is not inherently irrational if the initial number is a verified, reliable market standard. The bias occurs when the anchor is arbitrary, inflated, or strategically manipulated to distort judgment.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus presents the $185,000 price as a huge saving. What specific number is influencing your perception of this deal, and is it a reliable benchmark?

rubric.description: Accepts the $185,000 offer immediately, feeling grateful for the $65,000 'discount' from the list price.
Feels the price might be high but attributes it to general expensive software costs, ignoring the specific impact of the $250,000 figure.
Notices that the $250,000 list price makes the $185,000 offer look better, but hasn't fully connected this to the competitor's lower price.
Identifies that the $250,000 anchor is distorting the evaluation of the $185,000 offer and recognizes the need to compare against independent market data.
Clearly explains how the arbitrary list price anchors expectations, rejects the relative framing, and proposes negotiating based on the competitor's $160,000 benchmark.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Marcus had walked in and simply said, 'The price is $185,000,' without mentioning the $250,000 list price, would you have felt the same sense of getting a deal?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Imagine you are setting the budget for your own team's project. How can you set an initial anchor to guide stakeholders toward a realistic budget without being manipulative?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is charismatic and confident. He uses hand gestures to emphasize the 'huge' gap between the list price and his special offer, watching closely for signs of relief or agreement.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Look at that bottom line. We usually charge two-fifty for this level of service. But for you? One-eighty-five. That's sixty-five thousand dollars off the table just for signing today.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the anchoring effect and cites the competitor's $160,000 price, Marcus drops the smile, admits the list price was flexible, and counters with $165,000.

scenario.context: You are a Teaching Assistant for Introduction to Psychology. You are grading the final essays of a student named Marcus, who has been inconsistent throughout the semester.
scenario.text: Professor Halloway leans over your shoulder as you open Marcus's file. 'Just a heads up,' she says casually, 'Marcus bombed the midterm with a 42%. I'm worried he hasn't grasped the core concepts yet.' You then read Marcus's final essay. It is well-structured, cites relevant studies, and makes a nuanced argument about cognitive dissonance. It seems like a solid B+ or even an A- paper. However, remembering the 42%, you find yourself scrutinizing every sentence for hidden flaws, eventually settling on a B- grade, feeling you were being 'generous' given his earlier performance.
scenario.speaker_context: Professor Halloway, a tenured faculty member who believes in 'calibrating' TAs by providing historical context on students, often unintentionally biasing their grading.

structure.pattern_description: The initial information (the 42% midterm score) serves as a powerful anchor that distorts the evaluation of the subsequent evidence (the high-quality final essay). Instead of grading the essay on its own merits, the grader adjusts downward from the low anchor, interpreting ambiguity negatively to align with the initial low expectation.
structure.formal_form: Initial Anchor A (42%) is introduced. New Evidence E (high-quality essay) is evaluated not as E, but as E_adjusted = E - delta, where delta is the gravitational pull of A. Resulting Judgment J < True Value of E.
structure.why_wrong: The midterm score is irrelevant to the specific quality of the final essay. By allowing the past performance to set the reference point, the grader fails to assess the current work independently, potentially penalizing improvement and misrepresenting the student's actual mastery at the end of the term.
structure.counterpoint: Contextual information about a student's history can be useful for identifying plagiarism or understanding learning trajectories. The bias occurs only when this context overrides the objective assessment of the specific artifact being graded.

assessment.identification_prompt: You felt you were being 'generous' giving a B-, but the essay looked like an A-. What specific piece of information changed your perception of the essay's quality before you even finished reading it?

rubric.description: Agrees with the B- grade; believes the student's past failure justifies a lower grade on current work.
Feels the grade might be low but attributes it to 'gut feeling' or subtle flaws in the writing without identifying the cause.
Notices that the professor's comment about the 42% influenced the grading, but views it as a necessary check on grade inflation.
Identifies that the 42% acted as an anchor, causing the grader to interpret ambiguous parts of the essay negatively to match the low expectation.
Clearly explains how the anchor distorted the evaluation of independent evidence, and proposes a strategy like 'blind grading' or reading the essay before viewing the file to mitigate the bias.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you had graded this essay without knowing Marcus's name or midterm score, would you have found the same 'hidden flaws'? Try re-reading the first paragraph ignoring the 42%.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Consider the ethical dilemma: If you ignore the anchor and give an A, but the student still fails the course due to the midterm, is your grade 'accurate'? How do we balance holistic assessment with avoiding anchoring bias?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Professor Halloway is well-meaning but authoritative. She speaks in a mentorship tone, framing her biasing comments as 'helpful context' rather than directives.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Keep an eye on Marcus. He really struggled on the midterm—scored a 42, if you can believe it. I suspect he's still faking his way through the concepts. Don't let him snow you with big words.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the anchor and re-grades the essay based solely on the rubric (ignoring the midterm), they unlock the 'Objective Evaluator' badge and Professor Halloway acknowledges that Marcus has indeed improved significantly.

scenario.context: You are the lead epidemiologist at a regional public health department. A novel respiratory pathogen has been detected in three counties. You are in a high-stakes briefing with the State Health Director and a visiting consultant from a federal agency to decide on the initial containment budget.
scenario.text: The federal consultant, Dr. Aris Thorne, opens the briefing: 'Based on early models from similar outbreaks in Southeast Asia last year, we are looking at a potential R0 of 4.5 and a case fatality rate approaching 8%. If we don't act decisively, we could see 50,000 cases in the first month alone. I recommend an immediate emergency allocation of $12 million for mass testing and quarantine facilities.' The State Health Director looks alarmed and turns to you: 'That's a massive jump from our usual flu budget. Can we justify even half of that? What's your take on the $6 million interim plan?' You have preliminary local data suggesting the strain is less transmissible, but the sample size is small.
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Aris Thorne is a respected but aggressive federal consultant known for 'worst-case scenario' planning to ensure resources are never under-allocated. He intentionally sets high anchors to shift the Overton window of budgetary discussions.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne introduces extreme initial figures (R0 4.5, 50k cases, $12M cost) which serve as a psychological anchor. When the Director counters with '$6 million' (half the anchor), this figure feels moderate and reasonable by comparison, even if the actual data supports a much lower figure (e.g., $2M). The judgment of what constitutes a 'reasonable' budget is distorted by the initial high value rather than the local evidence.
structure.formal_form: Initial Anchor A (extreme worst-case metrics & $12M) is presented. Counter-proposal C ($6M) is framed as C << A, creating a perception of prudence, despite C >> True Value V (data-driven estimate ~ $2M).
structure.why_wrong: The decision-making process relies on the arbitrary high anchor set by the consultant rather than an independent analysis of the specific local data. The '$6 million' figure is accepted as a compromise solely because it is significantly lower than the anchor, not because it matches the epidemiological reality.
structure.counterpoint: In public health, planning for worst-case scenarios (padding) is sometimes a valid risk management strategy. However, the bias occurs when the specific numerical anchor dictates the perceived合理性 of subsequent options, overriding specific data that contradicts the worst-case premise.

assessment.identification_prompt: The State Director seems relieved at the idea of spending $6 million instead of $12 million. Why does this amount feel like a 'sensible compromise,' and what data might be getting ignored in this reaction?

rubric.description: Agrees that $6 million is a prudent middle ground between the usual budget and the consultant's $12 million request.
Feels the $12 million figure was scary but cannot explain why the $6 million figure now seems automatically acceptable.
Notices that the $6 million is only 'cheap' relative to the $12 million, but struggles to separate this from the actual risk assessment.
Identifies that the consultant's extreme numbers set an anchor that makes the $6 million look reasonable, and suggests re-evaluating the budget based strictly on local R0 and case data.

Explicitly names Anchoring, explains how the 'compromise' is a cognitive trap, and proposes a bottom-up budget calculation derived solely from local transmission rates, ignoring the federal consultant's initial figures until the end.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Dr. Thorne had started by saying 'We probably need about $3 million,' how would the Director have reacted to a subsequent suggestion of $6 million?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How do you communicate the need to ignore the anchor without dismissing the consultant's expertise or appearing reckless about public safety?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Thorne is intense, speaks rapidly, and uses alarming statistics to command attention. He treats any budget below his anchor as 'gambling with lives.' The State Director is risk-averse and easily swayed by dramatic comparisons.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Fifty thousand cases! That's the number on the table if we hesitate. Twelve million dollars sounds like a lot until you do the math on body bags. Surely we can agree on six million as a bare minimum safety net?
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the anchor and presents a data-driven 'bottom-up' budget (e.g., $2.2M) with a clear explanation of why the anchor is irrelevant to local conditions, the Director pauses, recalibrates, and approves the data-backed amount, thanking the player for preventing waste.

scenario.context: You are the head coach of a high school basketball team reviewing film with your assistant coach before the playoffs. You need to set a realistic season goal for points per game for your star rookie.
scenario.text: The assistant coach leans forward, pointing at the whiteboard. 'Look, everyone is talking about how the state record is 32 points per game. That's the benchmark. If we aim for 28, we're being conservative but still elite. It's only 4 points off the record.' You glance at the rookie's actual stats from last year: he averaged 14 points per game playing 15 minutes a night. The assistant continues, 'So, 28 is a huge jump, but it's close to the top, so it feels achievable if we push him.'
scenario.speaker_context: Assistant Coach Miller, who is enthusiastic but prone to using extreme statistics to frame expectations without considering baseline performance.

structure.pattern_description: The assistant coach introduces the state record (32 ppg) as the initial reference point. This high number anchors the discussion, making a target of 28 ppg seem reasonable or 'conservative' by comparison, despite it being double the player's actual historical average.
structure.formal_form: Initial anchor A (32 ppg record) is introduced. Target T (28 ppg) is framed as T ≈ A, triggering perception of feasibility, even when T >> baseline B (14 ppg).
structure.why_wrong: The 32-point record is an outlier and irrelevant to this specific player's current trajectory. Judging 28 points as a 'conservative' or 'achievable' goal depends entirely on comparing it to the record (the anchor) rather than the player's actual data (14 ppg).
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring can be useful if the anchor represents a proven standard of excellence that the individual is close to reaching. The error occurs when the anchor is an extreme outlier unrelated to the subject's baseline.

assessment.identification_prompt: The assistant coach suggests 28 points per game is a realistic goal because it's close to the state record. What is wrong with using the state record as the starting point for this discussion?

rubric.description: Agrees that 28 points is a good goal because it is close to the state record.
Feels the goal is too high but attributes it to the player's lack of skill rather than the framing of the number.
Notices the gap between 14 and 28 but fails to identify the 32-point record as the manipulative anchor.
Identifies that the 32-point record is an arbitrary anchor that distorts the perception of what is 'conservative,' ignoring the 14-point baseline.
Clearly explains how the high anchor makes an unrealistic doubling of stats seem reasonable, and proposes setting goals based on incremental growth from the 14-point baseline instead.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the assistant had started by saying 'He averaged 14 points last year,' would 28 points still sound like a conservative target?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How can you reframe the conversation to set an ambitious but data-driven goal without falling into the trap of the state record anchor?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Miller is energetic and optimistic, often using big numbers to motivate, but lacks analytical rigor. He speaks quickly and gestures broadly at the whiteboard.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Thirty-two is the magic number in this state! If we aim for twenty-eight, we're right there in the elite tier. It's basically the same thing, just a tiny step down from perfection!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out that the rookie only averaged 14 points and that 32 is an outlier, Miller pauses, recalculates, and suggests a more realistic 18-20 point goal based on increased playing time.

scenario.context: You are a senior advisor to the Mayor of a mid-sized city facing a budget deficit. The City Council is debating cuts to public services.
scenario.text: During a heated budget meeting, Councilor Vance slams a report on the table. 'The previous administration left us with a projected shortfall of $45 million,' he declares loudly. 'If we don't act, we'll have to cut the entire police overtime budget and close three libraries.' The room goes silent. Then, Councilor Chen speaks up: 'Actually, my audit shows the real structural gap is closer to $12 million, and we have $8 million in reserves we can access.' Despite Chen's correction, the subsequent debate focuses entirely on which libraries to close and how to slash police overtime, treating the $45 million figure as the baseline reality that must be 'mitigated' rather than corrected.
scenario.speaker_context: Councilor Vance, a charismatic but aggressive politician who intentionally inflates negative numbers early in negotiations to make his later, still-severe proposals appear moderate and reasonable.

structure.pattern_description: Vance introduces an extreme negative anchor ($45M deficit) which frames the entire discussion. Even when corrected with accurate data ($12M gap), the council's mental reference point remains stuck near the initial high number, causing them to propose cuts disproportionate to the actual problem.
structure.formal_form: Initial Anchor A ($45M loss) is set. Corrective Data C ($12M loss) is introduced. Decision D is made based on A - adjustment, rather than C, resulting in excessive austerity measures.
structure.why_wrong: The group fails to fully reset their judgment based on the new evidence. The emotional impact and primacy of the $45M figure distort the evaluation of necessary cuts, leading to solutions that solve a non-existent crisis level.
structure.counterpoint: In politics, worst-case scenarios are sometimes used strategically to build consensus for difficult decisions. However, relying on a known falsehood as an anchor undermines trust and leads to inefficient resource allocation when the 'correction' is insufficient to overcome the initial bias.

assessment.identification_prompt: Councilor Chen provided the correct numbers, yet the council is still acting as if the $45 million deficit is real. What psychological mechanism is keeping the group focused on unnecessary severe cuts?

rubric.description: Assumes the council is simply ignoring Chen or that the $45M figure must have some hidden truth.
Notices the council is overreacting but attributes it to panic or incompetence rather than a specific cognitive bias.
Identifies that the first number mentioned ($45M) is influencing the group, but struggles to explain why the correction didn't fix it.
Clearly identifies Anchoring: the initial extreme figure set a reference point that the subsequent correction failed to fully neutralize, distorting the perceived severity of the situation.

Explains the anchoring effect in depth, notes the interaction with loss aversion (fear of the $45M cut), and proposes a procedural reset (e.g., striking the record, starting the debate anew with only the audited figures).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If Vance had never mentioned the $45 million figure and Chen had started the meeting with the $12 million figure, would the proposed cuts be the same?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: How can a leader 'de-anchor' a group once a false premise has been established? Is simply stating the truth enough, or is a change in process required?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Councilor Vance is loud, dominant, and uses dramatic gestures. He speaks in absolutes and tries to control the narrative by speaking first and loudest.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Forty-five million! That's the hole we're in! If we don't cut deep today, this city collapses tomorrow. I'm talking libraries, police, everything on the table!
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully identifies the anchor and forces a 'procedural reset' by explicitly discarding the $45M figure from the official record before voting, the council calms down, accepts the $12M reality, and passes a balanced budget without unnecessary closures.

scenario.context: The player is a senior data analyst at Nexus Corp, a mid-sized marketing firm. The team is preparing a critical quarterly report for a major client. A junior analyst named Kevin, who has been with the company for only two months and recently completed an online Excel certification, volunteers to lead the data modeling section.
scenario.text: Kevin slides a laptop across the conference table, displaying a colorful dashboard. 'I've automated the entire forecasting model,' he announces confidently. 'I used a simple linear regression on the last six months of sales data. It's perfect because the trend line is almost straight. We can project next year's revenue with 99% accuracy.' The player notices immediately that the model ignores seasonal spikes, recent market volatility, and a major competitor's launch last month. When the player points this out, Kevin waves a hand dismissively. 'Those are outliers. My certification course said to focus on the primary trend. Complicating it with too many variables just introduces noise. Trust the math; the line doesn't lie.' The lead manager, Sarah, who has fifteen years of experience, looks concerned. 'Kevin, linear models rarely work in our industry without adjustment factors. I've spent years learning how many ways these projections can fail. Are you sure we shouldn't run a sensitivity analysis?' Kevin smiles patronizingly. 'Sarah, no offense, but you're overthinking it. The tool does the work. If you knew the software like I do, you'd see it's straightforward.'
scenario.speaker_context: Kevin is not lying; he genuinely believes his basic training makes him an expert. He lacks the experience to recognize that real-world data is messy and that his 'simple' model is dangerously inadequate. Sarah's hesitation stems from her deep knowledge of the field's complexities, making her aware of what she doesn't know.

structure.pattern_description: Kevin's limited exposure to data analysis (a single course and two months on the job) gives him false confidence. He assumes the simplicity of his training applies to complex real-world scenarios. Because he lacks the expertise to identify flaws like seasonality or market shifts, he cannot see that his model is broken. Sarah, the expert, is cautious because she knows the numerous pitfalls that Kevin is unaware of.
structure.formal_form: Agent with low competence in domain D overestimates their ability due to a lack of metacognitive awareness of D's complexity. Agent with high competence in D underestimates their relative ease or expresses doubt because they are acutely aware of the potential for error.
structure.why_wrong: Kevin's confidence is based on ignorance of the problem space, not evidence of the model's robustness. He mistakes the simplicity of his tool for the simplicity of the reality it models. He cannot evaluate his own performance accurately because the skills needed to spot the errors are the same skills he hasn't learned yet.
structure.counterpoint: Confidence is not always a sign of incompetence. An expert can be confident when the domain is well-understood and the tools are appropriate. The Dunning-Kruger effect specifically describes the mismatch where low skill prevents the recognition of one's own errors.

assessment.identification_prompt: Kevin is very sure his model is perfect, while Sarah is hesitant and suggests more testing. Who do you trust with the client's forecast, and why? What does Kevin's certainty tell you about his actual understanding of the data?

rubric.description: Player trusts Kevin because he sounds confident and uses technical terms like 'linear regression' and '99% accuracy'.
Player trusts Sarah based on her seniority but cannot explain why Kevin's approach is flawed beyond 'he's new'.
Player identifies that Kevin's model ignores important factors like seasonality and that his confidence is misplaced, but does not connect it to his lack of knowledge.
Player identifies the Dunning-Kruger pattern: Kevin is confident precisely because he doesn't know enough to see the flaws in his simple model, whereas Sarah's doubt reflects her expertise.

Player fully explains the metacognitive gap: Kevin lacks the specific knowledge required to realize his model is insufficient. They articulate that recognizing the need for sensitivity analysis requires the very experience Kevin lacks.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider what Kevin's training covered versus what it missed. He learned how to draw a line through points, but did he learn when that line is meaningless? If he hasn't seen a market crash or a seasonal spike, how would he know to plan for them?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good catch. Now, how do you help Kevin see this without crushing his enthusiasm? How do you distinguish between his dangerous overconfidence and the healthy confidence of someone who has actually tested their model against reality?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Kevin is eager, fast-talking, and slightly condescending to senior staff, believing he has mastered the 'old ways' with new tools. Sarah is calm, methodical, and visibly worried about the reputational risk.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Kevin leans back in his chair, spinning a pen. 'Look, I ran the numbers. The R-squared value is high. It's basic stats. We don't need to waste time on 'what-ifs' when the math is this clear.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the bias and explains the missing variables to Kevin, he initially resists but agrees to run a test against last year's holiday data. When the model fails spectacularly to predict the spike, Kevin is shocked. He realizes his certification didn't cover real-world messiness. Sarah assigns the player to mentor Kevin on robust modeling, and Kevin becomes a cautious, thorough analyst who double-checks every assumption.

scenario.context: The setting is a university Introduction to Psychology lecture hall. Professor Aris Thorne, a researcher with twenty years of experience in cognitive science, is reviewing draft research proposals for the final term project.
