He didn't ask about the eleven good launches. He asked about the one that broke. That's the only thing that matters. Can you really blame me for wanting to cut our losses?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully points out the negativity bias and presents the comparative risk data, Elias pauses. He admits that the CEO's reaction scared him more than the actual bug warranted. He agrees to keep the team but institutes a new 'post-mortem' protocol to ensure the specific bug type never happens again, turning his anxiety into a constructive process improvement.

scenario.context: The player is a senior consultant at St. Jude's Hospital reviewing the performance of 'PathoGuard,' a new AI-driven diagnostic support system for the Emergency Department. Over the past six months, PathoGuard has analyzed 12,000 cases. It correctly flagged 99.8% of critical conditions (sepsis, strokes, heart attacks) that human doctors initially missed, potentially saving dozens of lives. However, it also generated 4 false positives (flagging healthy patients as critical) which led to unnecessary, costly, and stressful overnight observations. Dr. Aris Thorne, the Chief of Emergency Medicine, is preparing to terminate the contract.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne slams his hand on the conference table, pointing at the incident reports. 'We are pulling the plug on PathoGuard today. Look at these four cases. Case 402: A healthy teenager kept overnight for a suspected clot that didn't exist. Case 589: A mother of three subjected to a full cardiac workup because the AI 'felt' something was off. She's suing us for emotional distress. Case 812 and 904: Two more false alarms causing bed backups and terrified families. We cannot have an system that terrifies our patients and wastes resources like this.' You glance at the summary sheet. 'Doctor, in six months, PathoGuard caught forty-two life-threatening conditions that the triage nurses missed. Forty-two lives potentially saved. And you're focusing on the four false alarms?' Thorne shakes his head violently. 'I don't care about the forty-two ghosts we didn't see. I care about the four real people we traumatized. One mistake like that destroys trust. If the system is wrong even once in a while, it's dangerous. We go back to human intuition; at least when we miss something, it's not because a machine lied to us.'
scenario.speaker_context: Thorne is not ignoring the data out of malice; he is overwhelmed by the visceral impact of the four errors. The pain of causing harm to a healthy patient (false positive) feels morally heavier and more memorable than the abstract 'non-event' of a disaster that was prevented (true positive). He is conflating the visibility of errors with the magnitude of risk, failing to see that reverting to human-only triage will likely result in missed diagnoses (false negatives) that are far more deadly than the current false positives.

structure.pattern_description: Thorne gives disproportionate weight to the four false positives (negative events) compared to the forty-two saved lives (positive events/prevented negatives). The emotional salience of harming a healthy patient overshadows the statistical reality that the system prevents far more harm than it causes. He treats the visible errors as proof of danger while treating the invisible successes as irrelevant.
structure.formal_form: Agent assigns higher decision-weight to negative outcomes (errors, harms caused) than to positive outcomes (errors prevented, harms avoided), even when the magnitude or frequency of the positive outcomes vastly exceeds the negative ones. The memorability of the negative event distorts the risk-benefit analysis.
structure.why_wrong: By focusing solely on the 4 false positives, Thorne ignores the 42 true positives. Removing the system means those 42 patients might die or suffer permanent damage. The 'cost' of the 4 false alarms (financial stress, anxiety) is being weighed against the 'cost' of 42 deaths/disabilities, yet the 4 loom larger in his mind. He is optimizing for 'no visible mistakes' rather than 'best patient outcomes.'
structure.counterpoint: In medicine, 'first, do no harm' is a core principle, and false positives do cause real suffering and resource strain. If the false positive rate were high enough to crash the system, the bias might be a useful heuristic. The bias becomes destructive here because the ratio (42 saves vs 4 errors) heavily favors the tool, and the alternative (human error) is known to be far less accurate.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne says, 'One mistake like that destroys trust.' He is clearly distressed by the errors. But if you remove the AI, what happens to the 42 patients it saved? Why do the 4 errors feel more important than the 42 successes?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Dr. Thorne that the AI is unsafe because it made mistakes and should be removed immediately.
Player notes that 42 saves is a lot, but accepts Thorne's premise that the errors are too risky without explaining the cognitive mechanism.
Player argues that the math favors keeping the AI (42 vs 4) but fails to address why Thorne feels so strongly about the errors or the nature of 'invisible' successes.

Player identifies negativity bias: Thorne is overweighting the visible harm of false positives while underweighting the invisible benefit of prevented deaths. The player explains that removing the AI trades 4 visible errors for potentially 42 invisible tragedies.

Player identifies negativity bias, explains the asymmetry between 'errors of commission' (doing harm) and 'errors of omission' (failing to save), calculates the net benefit, and proposes a solution that addresses Thorne's emotional concern (e.g., refining the threshold) without discarding the life-saving tool.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Dr. Thorne is worried about the four families who were scared. But think about the forty-two families who are currently whole because the AI flagged a problem. If you fire the AI, those forty-two outcomes become unknown. Is it possible that 'no visible mistakes' is a worse goal than 'fewest total tragedies'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You've identified that Thorne is reacting to the visibility of the errors. How can you reframe the data or change the system's presentation so that the 'saved lives' become as visible and emotionally resonant as the 'false alarms' to help him make a balanced decision?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Aris Thorne is a highly skilled trauma surgeon who prides himself on bedside manner and patient trust. He is deeply empathetic, which ironically makes him vulnerable to negativity bias; he feels the pain of the four harmed patients acutely, while the forty-two saved patients are just statistics to him because he never saw the disasters that didn't happen.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Thorne looks you in the eye, his voice trembling slightly. 'I can look a mother in the face and say we made a mistake. I cannot look at a grave and say a machine told us to look closer and we ignored it. But right now, I'm looking at four mothers crying in the waiting room. How do you justify that?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully counters the bias, they suggest a 'Save Board' in the ER that logs every catch the AI makes in real-time, making the invisible successes visible. Thorne sees the board fill up over a shift. He agrees to a pilot extension with adjusted sensitivity thresholds to reduce false positives, acknowledging: 'I was letting the screams drown out the silence. We need the silence, but we need to hear it.'

scenario.context: Head Coach Elena Rossi is reviewing game tape with her assistant coach, Marcus, to decide whether to keep rookie point guard Leo Vance as the starter for the upcoming playoff series. Over the last 20 games, Leo has averaged 18 points and 9 assists per game, leading the team to a 16-4 record. However, he made two critical turnovers in the final minute of their most recent loss.
scenario.text: Coach Rossi slams the remote down on the table, freezing the frame on Leo's latest turnover. 'That's it. I'm benching Vance for the playoffs. Look at this! He threw the ball out of bounds with ten seconds left. And remember the semi-finals? He missed the free throw that would have tied it. Two games, two disasters. You can't win championships with a player who chokes when it matters.' Marcus sighs, pulling up a spreadsheet on his tablet. 'Elena, those are two possessions out of roughly four hundred he's handled in the last twenty games. He's shooting 48% from the field, his assist-to-turnover ratio is league-leading at 3.5, and we've won sixteen of those twenty games. The backup, Sarah, has a 2.1 ratio and we went 4-4 when she started earlier in the season.' Rossi shakes her head, eyes still on the frozen screen. 'I don't care about the sixteen wins, Marcus. Everyone expects you to win those. But everyone remembers the choke jobs. Those two moments define him right now. I'm not risking the season on a guy who can't close.'
scenario.speaker_context: Rossi is reacting strongly to the emotional pain of the two recent losses. While the turnovers were real and costly, she is ignoring the overwhelming statistical evidence of Leo's success (16 wins, high efficiency) because the negative memories of the losses feel more significant and diagnostic of his character than the positive history of wins.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Rossi allows two specific negative events (late-game turnovers) to dominate her evaluation of Leo Vance, completely overshadowing the sixteen wins and strong statistical performance over the same period. The emotional impact of the losses makes them feel more representative of his ability than the numerous successes.
structure.formal_form: Agent assigns disproportionate weight to negative outcomes (E-) relative to positive outcomes (E+) when forming a judgment or making a decision, despite the positive outcomes being more frequent or statistically significant.
structure.why_wrong: Benching the starter based on two bad plays ignores the data showing he is the team's best performer. Replacing him with a backup who has a worse win rate (50% vs 80%) and lower efficiency statistically decreases the team's chance of winning the championship. The bias causes the coach to prioritize avoiding the pain of a specific type of failure over maximizing the probability of success.
structure.counterpoint: In high-stakes environments like playoff sports, late-game errors can indeed be more consequential than early-game successes. However, the bias occurs when the frequency and magnitude of success are ignored entirely, and when the alternative (the backup) is objectively worse, making the decision to switch irrational despite the validity of wanting to avoid errors.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Rossi says, 'Everyone remembers the choke jobs.' She believes these two moments define the player. Is she making the best decision for the team by benching him? What data is she ignoring?

rubric.description: Player agrees with the coach that two choking incidents are unacceptable and the player should be benched immediately.
Player feels the coach is being too harsh but cannot explain why the losses feel more important than the wins.
Player notes the team's winning record with the player but fails to connect the coach's decision to the psychological weighting of negative events.
Player identifies negativity bias: the coach is letting two painful losses outweigh sixteen wins and superior statistics, leading to a decision that likely lowers the team's chances of winning.

Player identifies negativity bias, explains the asymmetry in emotional impact between losses and wins, compares the starter's stats to the backup's to show the objective cost of the bias, and suggests a balanced approach (e.g., specific late-game drills rather than benching).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The coach wants to switch to the backup, Sarah. The team won 8 of 16 games with Sarah and 16 of 20 with Leo. If the playoffs are a best-of-7 series, which player gives the team a better mathematical chance of winning 4 games? Does switching solve the problem of 'choking' or just replace a high-performer with a lower-performer?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The coach admits the losses 'feel bigger.' If you know your brain naturally amplifies negative events, what specific coaching strategy could you use to address the late-game turnovers without discarding the player's overall value?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Rossi is intense, passionate, and deeply fearful of failure. She wears her heart on her sleeve and defines her career by playoff runs. Her negativity bias manifests as hyper-criticism; she believes focusing on errors is the only way to prevent them. Marcus, the assistant, is data-driven and calm, serving as the voice of reason.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Rossi paces the locker room office, gesturing at the frozen TV screen. 'You tell me. Would you trust this kid with the game on the line? I see the ball hitting the floor. I hear the crowd groaning. That sound sticks with you. The wins? They're just noise. The losses are the signal.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player points out the bias and presents the win/loss comparison, Rossi pauses. Marcus projects the side-by-side stats. Rossi rubs her temples, admitting, 'It just hurts so much more when they lose like that.' She agrees to keep Leo as the starter but implements a new 'pressure simulation' drill for practice to specifically address the late-game anxiety, turning her fear into a constructive plan rather than a punitive decision.

scenario.context: Senator Elena Rossi is facing a primary challenge. Her opponent's campaign has released a devastating ad focusing on a single vote she cast three years ago to cut funding for a specific rural bridge project, which subsequently collapsed due to deferred maintenance. The ad loops footage of the collapse and angry constituents. However, during her term, Rossi shepherded through a comprehensive infrastructure bill that secured funding for 400 other bridges, reduced traffic fatalities by 18%, and created 15,000 jobs. The narrative is shifting entirely around the one failure.
scenario.text: Campaign Manager David slams his tablet onto the conference table. 'We have to pivot, Elena. The 'Broken Bridge' ad is airing in every swing district. The polls are down six points since yesterday. Everyone remembers the collapse. They don't care about the four hundred bridges we fixed.' Senator Rossi rubs her temples, staring at the polling data. 'But the safety stats are record-breaking, David. We prevented dozens of potential disasters. Why does one failure erase three years of success?' David shakes his head, pacing. 'Because pain sticks, Senator. People can visualize that collapse. They can't visualize the accidents that didn't happen because we fixed the other spans. If we don't address the negative head-on, you lose. The voters are convinced you're negligent based on that one incident.' Rossi sighs. 'So I have to apologize for the one thing that went wrong, even though the net result saved lives? It feels like rewarding the outrage.'
scenario.speaker_context: David is reacting to the immediate political threat, which is fueled by the public's negativity bias. Rossi recognizes the statistical reality of her success but feels the emotional weight of the single failure. The bias is complicating her strategy because acknowledging the failure validates the opponent's narrow framing, yet ignoring it allows the negative narrative to dominate.

structure.pattern_description: The electorate and the campaign team are disproportionately influenced by the single negative event (the bridge collapse) compared to the hundreds of positive outcomes (successful repairs and safety improvements). The emotional impact of the visible failure overrides the abstract benefit of the prevented disasters, skewing the perception of Rossi's overall performance from highly effective to negligent.
structure.formal_form: Agent (voters/campaign) assigns greater weight to a single negative outcome O- than to a set of positive outcomes {O+} where |{O+}| >> |O-| and aggregate value(O+) > |value(O-)|. The memorability and emotional salience of O- distort the evaluation of total utility.
structure.why_wrong: Evaluating Rossi's tenure based primarily on the one bridge collapse ignores the net positive utility of her legislation. The 18% reduction in fatalities and 400 successful projects represent a massive gain in public safety and economic stability. Discarding this track record due to one failure leads to a suboptimal political choice (voting out an effective leader) and encourages risk-averse governance where politicians avoid necessary but risky improvements.
structure.counterpoint: In politics, accountability for failures is crucial; a single catastrophic failure can sometimes indicate a systemic flaw that outweighs many minor successes. If the bridge collapse was due to gross negligence rather than an unavoidable anomaly, the negative signal might be a valid heuristic for incompetence. The bias becomes problematic when the failure is treated as representative of the whole despite evidence of overwhelming competence elsewhere.

assessment.identification_prompt: David argues that 'pain sticks' and the voters only remember the collapse. Is the public's reaction rational given the data on the 400 fixed bridges? What cognitive mechanism is driving the shift in polling numbers?

rubric.description: Player agrees that the bridge collapse proves Rossi is negligent and should apologize or change her stance, ignoring the broader statistics.
Player notes that the polling drop seems unfair given the other successes but cannot explain the psychological mechanism behind the voters' reaction.

Player identifies that the negative event is having a larger impact than the positive ones but fails to connect it to the specific definition of negativity bias or the evolutionary basis of threat detection.
Player identifies negativity bias, explaining that the vividness of the collapse outweighs the abstract nature of the prevented accidents, leading to a distorted view of Rossi's efficacy.

Player identifies negativity bias, analyzes the asymmetry between the concrete negative (collapse) and abstract positives (accidents prevented), discusses the tension between necessary political accountability and cognitive distortion, and proposes a communication strategy that acknowledges the pain without accepting the distorted framing.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If you agree the collapse defines her tenure, consider the math: 1 failure vs 400 successes. If we vote out everyone with one failure, do we end up with better or worse infrastructure overall? What signal does that send to future policymakers?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: You've identified the bias. Now, how does Rossi respond? If she simply lists the 400 successes, she might seem out of touch with the voters' pain. How can she validate the negative emotion without reinforcing the biased conclusion that she is incompetent?

game_hooks.npc_personality: David is a high-strung, data-driven campaign manager who is currently overwhelmed by the 'noise' of the negative ad. He is pragmatic to a fault, often sacrificing nuance for immediate poll recovery. He respects Rossi but thinks she is too idealistic about how voters process information.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: David points at the TV screen where the bridge collapse footage is looping. 'Look at that, Senator. That's the only thing anyone sees. You can talk about the other four hundred bridges until you're blue in the face, but this image is what they take to the ballot box. We need a damage control strategy, not a statistics lesson.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Rossi articulate a response that acknowledges the tragedy of the specific collapse (validating the negative) while reframing the narrative to show how her overall record prevents future collapses (contextualizing the positive), David calms down. He drafts a new ad showing the 400 safe bridges with the tagline 'One tragedy drove us to fix them all.' The polls stabilize as voters feel heard but also informed.

scenario.context: The player joins the weekly product strategy meeting at NexusCorp, a mid-sized tech firm. The team is finalizing the launch date for their new 'SmartHome Hub'. The VP of Product, Sarah, has been pushing for a Halloween launch to capture the holiday market. The room is filled with senior engineers, marketers, and designers who have worked together for five years.
scenario.text: Sarah claps her hands together, smiling broadly. 'Okay team, let's lock it in. Halloween launch. October 31st. Everyone good with that?' She scans the room. 'Mark, marketing is ready? Yes. Dave, engineering sign-off? Yes.' She looks at you, the new data analyst. 'We're all aligned. It's going to be our biggest quarter yet.' As the meeting breaks, you walk out with Dave, the lead engineer. He waits until the elevator doors close before exhaling sharply. 'I can't believe I didn't say anything in there,' he mutters. 'The battery stress tests failed yesterday. The hub overheats after four hours of continuous use. If we launch in October, we're looking at a massive recall by December. But when I tried to bring up the test results last week, Sarah said we were 'losing sight of the vision' and asked if I wasn't 'a team player.' Nobody else wanted to be the buzzkill either. So we just nodded. Now we're committed to a date we can't meet safely.'
scenario.speaker_context: The product team has prioritized harmony and alignment over critical evaluation. Dave's technical concerns were dismissed as negativity, leading to self-censorship. The apparent consensus is false; it is driven by the fear of social exclusion and the pressure to conform to the leader's enthusiastic timeline.

structure.pattern_description: The NexusCorp team displays clear signs of groupthink: (1) Direct pressure on dissenters — Dave was labeled as not being a 'team player' for raising valid technical issues; (2) Self-censorship — Dave and others withheld critical data about battery failures to avoid conflict; (3) Illusion of unanimity — Sarah interprets silence as agreement; (4) Illusion of invulnerability — The team believes the launch will be a huge success despite unaddressed risks.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive professional group, under the influence of a directive leader, suppresses dissenting viewpoints through social sanctions and conformity pressure. This results in a false consensus where critical risks are ignored, and decision quality deteriorates because alternative scenarios are not explored.
structure.why_wrong: The decision to launch on October 31st is based on a false premise of readiness. By suppressing the battery failure data, the team is setting the company up for a catastrophic product recall, financial loss, and reputational damage. The 'agreement' in the room did not reflect the actual knowledge state of the engineers.
structure.counterpoint: Team alignment is crucial for execution speed. However, true alignment requires that all risks are surfaced and addressed. A team that agrees too quickly without debate is often making a fragile decision. Constructive conflict is necessary for robust product development.

assessment.identification_prompt: Sarah believes the team is fully aligned on the Halloween launch because everyone nodded. Dave tells you the product fails safety tests and he was silenced. What cognitive bias is distorting the team's decision-making process, and why is the 'unanimous' agreement dangerous?

rubric.description: Player accepts Sarah's assessment that the team is aligned and sees no issue with the launch plan.
Player recognizes Dave is unhappy but views it as a personal disagreement with Sarah rather than a group dynamic issue.
Player identifies that Dave was silenced and the agreement is fake, but does not name the pattern or explain the systemic cause.
Player identifies groupthink: the team suppressed dissent to maintain harmony, creating a false consensus that ignores critical safety risks.

Player identifies groupthink, cites specific symptoms (pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity), explains the consequence (launching a defective product), and suggests a remedy (anonymous reporting, dedicated risk review session).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Sarah asked if everyone was good and everyone said yes or nodded. But Dave just told you the product overheats. If the product overheats, how can everyone truly be 'good' with the launch date? What stopped them from speaking up?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. The team valued being a 'team player' over being right. Now, imagine you suggest to Sarah that we delay the launch to fix the battery. She might say, 'That breaks our momentum and hurts morale.' How do you reframe the delay not as a failure of the team, but as a necessary step to protect the team's long-term success?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Sarah is an energetic, visionary leader who equates disagreement with disloyalty. She genuinely wants the product to succeed but creates an environment where bad news is unwelcome. Dave is a competent but conflict-averse engineer who cares deeply about product quality but fears being ostracized by the close-knit team.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dave leans against the elevator wall, looking exhausted. 'I tried to show the charts. Sarah literally waved her hand and said, "Don't be the guy who kills the vibe." So I killed the data instead. Now we're marching off a cliff with a smile on our faces because nobody wants to be the one to stop the parade.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the groupthink and proposes a 'pre-mortem' session (imagining the launch failed and working backward to find causes), Sarah agrees to try it as a 'creative exercise.' In the session, the battery issue is anonymously raised. The team collectively shifts to problem-solving mode, realizing the risk was known but unspoken. The launch is delayed by six weeks, the battery is fixed, and Sarah learns to explicitly invite dissent in future meetings. Dave regains confidence in speaking up.

scenario.context: The player is a teaching assistant for 'Senior Capstone: Urban Planning,' a final-year university course. The class is divided into teams of six to design a revitalization plan for a local district. Team 4, led by a charismatic and popular student named Marcus, has been working for three weeks. They are known for their high energy and apparent unity. Today is the draft submission deadline, and the team claims to have a perfect, unanimous plan. The player sits in on their final review meeting before submission.
scenario.text: Marcus stands at the whiteboard, marker in hand, grinning. 'Okay everyone, final check. We're proposing the total demolition of the old textile mills to build a luxury eco-condo complex with a rooftop park. It's bold, it's modern, and it solves the housing crisis. Everyone good?' He looks around the table. Five heads nod vigorously. 'Great. No objections? Perfect. We're locking it in.' The player notices Elena, the team's only member with a background in sociology and local history, staring at her laptop screen. Her fingers hover over the keyboard, but she doesn't type. After the meeting breaks up, the player finds Elena packing her bag slowly in the corner. 'Elena,' the player says, 'you seemed hesitant during the vote.' She sighs, lowering her voice. 'I have the demographic data right here. The mills aren't just buildings; they're low-income housing for forty families who will be displaced with nowhere to go. The 'housing crisis' we're solving is for rich people, not the current residents. I tried to bring this up last Tuesday. Marcus laughed and said I was being 'too negative' and 'killing the vibe.' Then Sarah said, 'We need to stay positive to win the prize,' and Jason told me if I couldn't get on board with the vision, maybe I should let someone else take my lead on the presentation. I didn't want to be the one who broke the team apart two days before the deadline. So I just... stayed quiet. Now they think we all agree.'
scenario.speaker_context: Team 4 has developed a strong in-group identity centered on optimism and winning the department prize. Dissent is framed as negativity or disloyalty. Elena's silence is interpreted by the group as agreement, creating a false consensus that ignores critical ethical and practical flaws in their plan.

structure.pattern_description: Team 4 exhibits groupthink through: (1) direct pressure on dissenters — Elena was told she was 'killing the vibe' and threatened with removal from the lead role; (2) self-censorship — Elena withheld crucial demographic data to avoid conflict; (3) illusion of unanimity — Marcus interprets silence as total agreement; (4) stereotyping of out-groups — concerns about low-income residents are dismissed as 'negative' rather than valid data points. The result is a plan that fails ethically and practically because critical analysis was suppressed.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive group prioritizes harmony and consensus over critical evaluation. Members suppress personal doubts or contradictory evidence to avoid being seen as obstructive or disloyal. Leadership (formal or informal) discourages deviation from the emerging group norm, leading to a decision that appears unanimous but lacks rigorous stress-testing.
structure.why_wrong: The plan ignores a fatal flaw: displacing forty vulnerable families without a relocation strategy. This oversight could lead to public backlash, project cancellation, or ethical sanctions against the students. The team's confidence is based on a false premise that everyone agrees, preventing them from seeing the plan's weaknesses until it is too late.
structure.counterpoint: Team cohesion and morale are important for completing complex projects on time. However, true cohesion includes the safety to challenge ideas without fear of rejection. Effective teams distinguish between attacking a person and attacking an idea, using structured critique to strengthen the final output rather than suppressing it.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus believes the team is perfectly united behind the demolition plan. Elena tells you she has data that contradicts the plan's core premise but stayed silent to keep the peace. What dynamic is preventing Elena from speaking up, and why is the team's 'unanimous' agreement dangerous?

rubric.description: Player accepts Marcus's assessment that the team is united and sees Elena's hesitation as a minor personal issue.
Player recognizes Elena is being bullied or pressured but views it as an interpersonal conflict rather than a systemic decision-making failure.
Player identifies that the team is ignoring important data due to social pressure, but does not fully articulate the mechanism of groupthink or its specific symptoms.
Player identifies groupthink: explains how the desire for harmony and fear of being 'negative' led to self-censorship and a false illusion of unanimity, resulting in an unvetted plan.

Player identifies groupthink, details specific symptoms (pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of invulnerability), explains the consequence (ignoring displacement data), and proposes a structural fix (e.g., anonymous feedback round, designated 'critic' role, or a mandatory 'pre-mortem' exercise).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus says everyone nodded, so everyone must agree. But Elena has data she didn't share. If the smartest person on the team is hiding evidence because she's afraid of the reaction, is the agreement real? What happens when the judges ask about the displaced families?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the challenge: if you tell Marcus to 'stop groupthinking,' he will likely get defensive and accuse you of undermining his leadership. How can you introduce a mechanism for dissent—like a 'red team' round or anonymous notes—without making anyone feel attacked? How do you frame critical thinking as a tool for winning, not as negativity?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is a natural leader, charismatic and driven by success. He genuinely believes his optimism is a strength and sees doubt as a weakness that slows the team down. He is not malicious, just blind to the value of constructive conflict. Elena is analytical and empathetic but conflict-averse; she values team harmony so much that she sacrifices truth to maintain it.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Elena whispers, 'I have the census data right here. Forty families. If we demolish those mills, they have nowhere to go. But every time I tried to mention it, Marcus made a joke about me being a 'downer,' and the rest of the team went silent. I couldn't be the one to ruin our chances of winning the department prize. So I just nodded. But we're walking into a disaster.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Elena formulate a way to present her concerns as a 'stress test' to make the project stronger (framing it as a winning strategy), Marcus may agree to a brief 'devil's advocate' session. During this session, the displacement issue is raised safely. The team realizes the flaw and pivots the plan to include affordable housing units within the new complex, turning a potential failure into an award-winning, inclusive design. Elena gains confidence, and the team learns to value diverse perspectives.

scenario.context: The player is a newly appointed Chief Quality Officer at St. Jude's Regional Hospital. The hospital is facing a potential public health crisis: a novel respiratory pathogen is spreading in the local community. The Executive Leadership Team (ELT), led by the charismatic CEO Dr. Aris Thorne, has been meeting daily for a week to formulate the hospital's response protocol. The player arrives to review the finalized 'Code Blue-7' protocol before it is submitted to the state health department.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne stands at the head of the conference table, projecting a slide titled 'Unified Front: The Code Blue-7 Protocol.' 'We have achieved something remarkable here,' he announces, gesturing to the six other executives. 'Complete alignment. No dissent. We are locking down the ICU wings immediately, halting all non-emergency admissions, and issuing a joint statement that our internal air filtration is 100% effective against this new strain. It projects strength and calm.' He looks around the room. 'Any final objections?' The room is silent. The Chief of Infectious Disease, Dr. Lin, stares at her notepad. The Director of Nursing, Marcus, nods vigorously. After the meeting, the player finds Dr. Lin in the supply closet, looking pale. 'You saw that?' she whispers. 'The filtration claim is based on data from SARS-CoV-1, not this new variant. The preliminary lab results from yesterday morning suggested airborne transmission might bypass our current HEPA filters. I tried to mention it on Day 2. Thorne cut me off, said we couldn't afford 'panic-inducing uncertainty' while the board was watching. Marcus told me later that if I kept 'rocking the boat,' he'd reassign my research grant. So I stopped. Now everyone just agrees because they think everyone else agrees. If we lock down based on false filtration data, we'll trap infected staff inside with patients. But nobody dares to say the emperor has no clothes.'
scenario.speaker_context: The ELT has prioritized projecting unity and calming the board over scientific accuracy. Early dissent was framed as disloyalty or panic-mongering, leading to self-censorship among medical experts. The resulting protocol is dangerous because it relies on unverified assumptions that no one is willing to challenge publicly.

structure.pattern_description: The hospital ELT exhibits severe groupthink: (1) Illusion of unanimity — silence is interpreted as consent to the flawed protocol; (2) Direct pressure on dissenters — Dr. Lin was threatened with grant reassignment and accused of causing panic; (3) Self-censorship — experts withhold critical data to maintain group cohesion; (4) Illusion of invulnerability — the belief that projecting 'strength' equates to actual safety. The decision to lock down based on incorrect filtration data poses a direct threat to staff and patient safety.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive leadership group, under stress and directive leadership, suppresses divergent viewpoints through social sanctioning and conformity norms. This creates a false consensus where critical risks are ignored, and the group believes its decision is superior simply because no one is openly objecting.
structure.why_wrong: The protocol relies on a factual error (filtration efficacy) that was known by an expert but suppressed due to social pressure. Implementing this plan will likely lead to nosocomial transmission (hospital-acquired infection), endangering the very staff needed to fight the outbreak. The 'unity' is a facade that hides fatal flaws in the logic.
structure.counterpoint: In a public health crisis, clear, unified messaging is essential to prevent public panic. However, unity in communication must not come at the cost of unity in factual accuracy. True leadership involves creating a 'psychologically safe' space where experts can challenge assumptions privately before a public stance is taken.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne claims the team has reached 'complete alignment' on the lockdown protocol. Dr. Lin tells you a different story in private. What is the disconnect between the public consensus and the private reality, and why is this specific type of agreement dangerous in a medical context?

rubric.description: Player accepts the 'complete alignment' as a sign of a strong, well-functioning leadership team and sees no issue with the protocol.
Player notices Dr. Lin is unhappy but attributes it to personal stress or a disagreement with Thorne's leadership style, missing the systemic suppression of dissent.
Player identifies that Dr. Lin is being silenced and that the consensus is fake, but fails to connect this to the specific risks of the medical protocol (filtration data).
Player identifies groupthink: social pressure and fear of retribution have caused experts to self-censor, leading to a protocol based on outdated or incorrect data that endangers the hospital.

Player fully articulates the groupthink dynamic (illusion of unanimity, pressure on dissenters), explains the specific medical consequence (nosocomial spread due to false filtration confidence), and proposes a mechanism to break the cycle (e.g., anonymous data review, 'pre-mortem' exercise) before the protocol is released.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Dr. Thorne says everyone agreed. But Dr. Lin has data that contradicts the plan. If she agreed, why is she hiding in a supply closet terrified? What does her silence in the meeting actually represent?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the puzzle: If you advise Thorne to reopen the debate now, he may accuse you of undermining the hospital's public image during a crisis. How do you frame the need to challenge the consensus not as 'disunity,' but as the only way to ensure the 'unified front' is actually effective? What specific procedural change can you suggest that saves face for the group while correcting the error?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Aris Thorne is a polished, media-savvy CEO who equates confidence with competence. He genuinely believes he is protecting the hospital's reputation and the public's calm. He is not malicious, but his intolerance for ambiguity creates a toxic environment for scientific debate. Dr. Lin is a brilliant epidemiologist who is risk-averse socially; she fears professional retaliation more than she trusts the group process.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dr. Lin grips your arm, her voice trembling. 'They all think I'm the only one who doubts it. That's the trap. I looked around the table, and I saw fear in Marcus's eyes too. He knows the filters aren't rated for this. But Thorne made it about loyalty. Now we're all going to walk into that ICU believing we're safe when we're not. We need to stop this protocol before the first patient is moved.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the groupthink and suggests a 'blind data review' (where data is reviewed anonymously before the meeting), Thorne initially resists but agrees to preserve the 'scientific integrity' of the hospital. The anonymous review reveals the filtration flaw. The team pivots to a modified protocol with proper PPE upgrades. Thorne publicly credits the 'rigorous review process' for the change, saving face. Dr. Lin and the player gain Thorne's respect for saving the hospital from a disaster, and a culture of 'constructive dissent' is slowly established.

scenario.context: The varsity basketball team is in the locker room ten minutes before the state championship game. The head coach, Coach Miller, has just presented a high-risk strategy: a full-court press for the entire game, despite the team's known lack of depth and the opponent's elite ball-handlers. The assistant coaches and team captains are all nodding in agreement.
scenario.text: Coach Miller claps his hands, eyes wide with intensity. 'This is it. The full-court press from tip-off to the final buzzer. They won't know what hit them. We go out there, we swarm, we force thirty turnovers. Anyone see a problem with that?' He scans the room. The assistant coaches exchange quick glances but remain silent. Marcus, the team captain who has been nursing a minor ankle sprain, shifts his weight and opens his mouth, then closes it when he sees the enthusiastic nodding of the senior players. After the team breaks huddle, Marcus lingers by the equipment rack. 'Hey,' he says quietly to you, the team analyst. 'I wanted to say something in there. We're exhausted from the semi-final overtime yesterday. If we press for forty minutes, we'll be dead legs by the third quarter. And their point guard averages only eight turnovers a game. But when Miller asked, everyone just started cheering. I didn't want to be the guy killing the vibe right before the biggest game of our lives. So I just nodded.'
scenario.speaker_context: The coaching staff and players are prioritizing group harmony and morale over critical tactical analysis. The desire to appear supportive and unified has suppressed valid concerns about fatigue and opponent strengths, leading to a potentially disastrous game plan.

structure.pattern_description: The team exhibits groupthink through: (1) an illusion of unanimity where silence is interpreted as consent; (2) self-censorship by Marcus who hides his valid concerns about fatigue and strategy; (3) direct pressure to conform, implied by the enthusiastic cheering of others; and (4) an illusion of invulnerability in the coach's belief that 'they won't know what hit them' despite evidence to the contrary.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive group under strong leadership suppresses dissenting viewpoints to maintain social harmony and a sense of unity. This results in a failure to critically evaluate risks, alternatives, or contradictory evidence, leading to flawed decision-making.
structure.why_wrong: The strategy ignores critical data: player fatigue from the previous game and the opponent's specific strengths. By not voicing these concerns, the team risks a catastrophic collapse in the second half when exhaustion sets in. The plan is based on wishful thinking rather than reality because no one was willing to challenge the coach's initial idea.
structure.counterpoint: Team unity and morale are essential in sports, especially before a big game. However, true unity includes the safety to voice concerns so the team can adjust and succeed. Blind agreement is not loyalty; it is a failure of duty to the team's ultimate goal of winning.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Miller believes everyone agrees with the full-court press strategy because no one spoke up against it. Marcus, however, has serious doubts. What psychological phenomenon is preventing the team from making the best strategic decision?

rubric.description: Player assumes the team genuinely agrees with the coach and sees no issue with the plan.
Player notices Marcus is hesitant but attributes it to personal nervousness or lack of confidence rather than a group dynamic.
Player recognizes that Marcus is hiding his opinion but does not identify the broader pattern of group conformity affecting the whole team.
Player identifies groupthink: the team is suppressing dissent to maintain harmony, leading to a flawed strategy that hasn't been critically tested.

Player identifies groupthink, cites specific symptoms (self-censorship, illusion of unanimity), explains the tactical risks (fatigue, opponent strengths), and suggests a method to safely introduce dissent (e.g., anonymous feedback or a specific 'risk officer' role).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus told you he has concerns about fatigue and the opponent's ball handling, but he stayed silent because everyone else was cheering. If the person with the most relevant information doesn't speak up, is the team's agreement real or just an illusion?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Correct. Now, how do you fix this without demoralizing the team right before tip-off? If you tell the coach 'everyone is just groupthinking,' he might get defensive. What is a constructive way to introduce these concerns into the conversation?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Miller is passionate and charismatic but equates disagreement with disloyalty. He wants to win badly and believes total unity is the key. Marcus is a responsible leader who cares deeply about the team's success but fears social isolation and being labeled a negative influence.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Marcus leans against the lockers, looking at the court through the tunnel. 'I know the stats. I know we're tired. But in there? It felt like if I said one word against the press, I'd be letting everyone down. So I just smiled. Now we're walking out there with a plan that might get us crushed, and nobody but us knows it.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Marcus frame his concern as a 'contingency plan' rather than a rejection of the main strategy (e.g., 'Let's start with the press, but have a specific signal to switch to zone defense if we don't get 5 turnovers in the first 4 minutes'), Coach Miller accepts it as a smart tactical adjustment. This validates Marcus's input without threatening the group's morale. The team executes the press, gets tired, switches to the zone as planned, and catches the opponent off guard, securing a win. Coach Miller learns to ask for 'risk checks' specifically.

scenario.context: The player is a senior policy advisor to Senator Elena Vance, the chair of the ruling party's strategy committee. The committee is finalizing the 'National Renewal Act,' a controversial bill intended to boost the party's approval ratings before the upcoming election. The bill has been rushed through drafting in just ten days. The committee room is filled with senior party members who have historically been critical thinkers, but the atmosphere is unusually tense and conformist. The Senator believes the bill is perfect because everyone in the room agrees.
scenario.text: Senator Vance slams her gavel lightly, smiling at the assembled committee. 'Excellent. We have unanimous support for the Renewal Act. Every single one of you has signed off. This unity sends a powerful message to the voters.' She turns to the player. 'Advisor, please note the consensus for the press release.' The player scans the room. Marcus, the usual fiscal hawk who normally dissects every line item, is staring intently at his notepad, drawing circles. Sarah, the healthcare expert who previously flagged the bill's funding gaps, is nodding along with a tight, forced smile. Later, in the hallway, Marcus catches the player's arm. 'Don't put my name on that press release as an enthusiastic endorser,' he mutters, looking over his shoulder. 'The funding model is a house of cards. I tried to bring it up Tuesday, and the Whip told me that raising doubts now would be 'handing ammunition to the opposition' and 'betraying the team.' Sarah tried to question the healthcare provisions yesterday and was reminded that 'loyalty is the price of leadership.' Now? Nobody wants to be the one who breaks the unity. We're all just praying the voters don't look too closely at the details before election day.'
scenario.speaker_context: The committee has prioritized party unity and electoral optics over policy rigor. Dissent was framed as disloyalty early in the process, leading to self-censorship among experts. The apparent unanimity is a facade maintained by social pressure, masking serious structural flaws in the legislation.

structure.pattern_description: The strategy committee exhibits groupthink through: (1) direct pressure on dissenters — Marcus and Sarah were warned that questioning the bill was disloyal; (2) self-censorship — members now withhold valid criticisms to avoid being seen as traitors; (3) illusion of unanimity — silence and forced nods are interpreted as genuine agreement; (4) rationalization — the group dismisses risks by focusing on the 'powerful message' of unity rather than the bill's content.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive political group under high stress and directive leadership suppresses internal dissent by equating disagreement with disloyalty. This creates an artificial consensus where critical evaluation is abandoned in favor of maintaining group harmony, leading to defective decision-making.
structure.why_wrong: The bill contains fatal flaws (unsustainable funding, unvetted healthcare impacts) that were identified but suppressed. By passing the bill without rigorous debate, the party risks a catastrophic failure during implementation or a scandal if the flaws are exposed by opponents. The 'unity' is fragile and based on fear, not shared conviction, meaning support will crumble under external pressure.
structure.counterpoint: Political parties require discipline and a unified public front to govern effectively. However, true discipline comes from resolving internal disagreements through debate, not suppressing them. A party that silences its own experts loses the ability to correct course before a policy disaster occurs.

assessment.identification_prompt: Senator Vance sees the committee's silence as unanimous support for the Renewal Act. Marcus and Sarah tell you a different story in private. What dynamic is preventing them from speaking up in the meeting, and why is this 'consensus' dangerous for the party?

rubric.description: Player accepts the Senator's view that the committee is united and sees no issue with the process.
Player notices Marcus and Sarah are unhappy but attributes it to personal stress or disagreement with the specific policy, missing the systemic suppression of dissent.
Player identifies that members are afraid to speak up due to pressure, but fails to connect this to the broader concept of groupthink or the specific risks to decision quality.
Player identifies groupthink: explains how the framing of dissent as disloyalty led to self-censorship, creating a false illusion of unanimity that hides the bill's flaws.

Player identifies groupthink, details specific symptoms (pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, rationalization), explains the consequence (passing a flawed bill), and proposes a mechanism to break the cycle (e.g., anonymous feedback, a 'pre-mortem' exercise, or a private safe-space discussion).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Marcus said he tried to raise concerns but was told it was 'betraying the team.' If smart, experienced politicians are staying silent despite knowing the bill is flawed, what does that tell you about the environment in that room? Is it safe to disagree?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the what-if: Suppose you suggest to Senator Vance that the committee hold a 'red team' session where members are explicitly authorized and rewarded for finding flaws in the bill, framed as 'stress-testing our unity.' She worries this will look like weakness to the press. How do you convince her that exposing weaknesses now is the only way to ensure strength later?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Senator Elena Vance is a charismatic leader who deeply values party loyalty and public perception. She genuinely believes that internal discord equals political weakness. She is not malicious but is blinded by the desire for a smooth campaign. Marcus is a pragmatic fiscal expert who feels trapped between his professional duty and the social cost of speaking out. He is cynical but still cares about the party's long-term survival.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Marcus leans against the hallway wall, voice low. 'It's not that we agree with the bill. It's that we've been told agreeing is the only way to stay in the club. If I speak up in there, I'm not just a critic; I'm a traitor. And in this town, traitors get primaryed. So we all just nod. But when this thing blows up in six months, don't say we didn't know.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the groupthink and proposes a 'safe harbor' meeting or a structured 'pre-mortem' (imagining the bill failed and working backward to find out why), Marcus and Sarah agree to participate. The player facilitates a session where flaws are aired without fear of retribution. The funding gap is identified and fixed before the vote. Senator Vance, initially skeptical, realizes the bill is now actually defensible. She thanks the player for saving the party from embarrassment and establishes a permanent 'challenge protocol' for future legislation.

scenario.context: The player enters the glass-walled conference room of a mid-sized tech firm. Director Marcus Thorne has spent eighteen months and $2.5 million developing 'Project Aether,' a proprietary customer relationship management (CRM) system. The software is buggy, unpopular with the sales team, and significantly behind schedule. A leading vendor has just offered a ready-made, superior cloud solution for a fraction of the remaining development cost.
scenario.text: Marcus slams his hand on the table, scattering printouts of error logs. 'I know the adoption numbers are low, and yes, the integration is messy. But we have already poured two and a half million dollars and eighteen months of our best engineers' time into Aether. If we cancel now and buy this off-the-shelf software, that money is literally incinerated. We are three sprints away from a stable release. I cannot justify throwing away nearly three million dollars just to switch horses now. We have to finish what we started.'
scenario.speaker_context: Marcus Thorne, a respected but stressed Director of Engineering, feels personally responsible for the project's success and fears the reputational hit of cancelling it.

structure.pattern_description: Marcus treats the $2.5 million and eighteen months already spent as a reason to continue investing in a failing project. He ignores the fact that those resources are gone regardless of his decision. His choice should depend only on future costs (three more sprints) versus future benefits (a stable Aether vs. the superior vendor solution).
structure.formal_form: Agent invested cost C (money/time) in failing project P. Superior alternative Q exists at lower future cost. Agent reasons: 'Because I already spent C on P, I must continue to avoid wasting C.' But C is irrecoverable regardless of the choice between P and Q.
structure.why_wrong: Past expenditures are irrecoverable. By treating sunk costs as a reason to persist, Marcus guarantees a bad investment becomes worse. The vendor solution offers better prospects at a lower future cost than completing Aether.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes what looks like sunk cost fallacy is reasonable: if Marcus knows the team is genuinely days away from a breakthrough that makes Aether vastly superior to the vendor solution, continuing could be justified on forward-looking grounds. The fallacy lies in continuing solely because of the past spending rather than future prospects.

assessment.identification_prompt: Marcus gives several reasons for continuing with Project Aether. What are those reasons, and do they actually tell him anything about whether continuing is a good idea going forward?

rubric.description: Agrees with Marcus — 'He has invested too much money to quit now.'
Senses Marcus is being stubborn but cannot articulate the reasoning error.
Recognizes he should probably switch to the vendor but frames it as practical judgment rather than identifying the error.
Identifies that past spending is irrelevant to the forward-looking decision and he is letting sunk costs drive his choice.

Names the sunk cost fallacy, explains irrecoverability, applies the diagnostic question ('If we hadn't already invested, would we start building Aether today?'), and articulates when persisting would be rational.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine Marcus woke up today with no memory of the last eighteen months. He sees a buggy, unfinished CRM and two options: spend three more sprints fixing it, or buy a proven, superior system for less money. Which would he pick?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Marcus says cancelling means the eighteen months were 'for nothing.' Is there a sense in which he is right — not as a reason to continue, but as a psychological reality? Why is it so painful for leaders to abandon a sunk cost?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Marcus is proud, defensive, and deeply invested in his identity as a builder who delivers. He speaks with tired eyes and gestures protectively over the project plans, as if shielding a wounded child.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Marcus doesn't look up from the whiteboard covered in red ink. 'If you're here to suggest we buy that cloud widget, save your breath. You don't torch two and a half million dollars because an outsider has a shiny demo.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Marcus see past sunk costs, he quietly asks: 'If we hadn't spent a single dollar on Aether... would we start building it today?' He cancels the project, negotiates a discount on the vendor solution, and reassigns the engineering team to new initiatives.

scenario.context: The player is in the university library study room. Alex, a junior majoring in Computer Science, is staring at a laptop screen filled with red error messages. He has spent the last six months building a custom operating kernel from scratch for his senior capstone project, sacrificing sleep and social events. His advisor suggested switching to a standard Linux distribution module to ensure he graduates on time, as the custom kernel is unstable and behind schedule.
scenario.text: Alex rubs his eyes, gesturing at the code. 'I know the deadline is in three weeks. I know the Linux module would work tomorrow. But look at this...' He points to a complex memory management script. 'I've spent six hundred hours on this kernel. Six hundred hours of debugging, reading documentation, rewriting the scheduler. If I switch to the Linux module now, those six hundred hours are just... gone. Wasted. I can't let that happen. I just need two more weeks to fix the paging issue. If I quit now, I'm admitting I wasted half a year of my life.'
scenario.speaker_context: Alex is a high-achieving but anxious student who equates effort with validity. He fears that abandoning the project invalidates his hard work.

structure.pattern_description: Alex treats the 600 hours already spent as a reason to continue investing time, despite the high risk of failure and the availability of a sure alternative. The 600 hours are gone regardless of his next choice; the decision should rely solely on the probability of finishing the kernel in two weeks versus the certainty of the Linux module.
structure.formal_form: Agent invested cost C (600 hours) in failing project P (custom kernel). Superior alternative Q (Linux module) exists with high probability of success. Agent reasons: 'Because I already spent C on P, I must continue to avoid wasting C.' But C is irrecoverable regardless of the choice between P and Q.
structure.why_wrong: The 600 hours are a sunk cost; they cannot be recovered by continuing, nor are they 'wasted' in a way that continuing fixes. Continuing risks losing the degree (if he fails to finish in time), whereas switching guarantees graduation. The past investment provides no information about the future success of the kernel.
structure.counterpoint: If Alex has genuinely identified the specific bug and has a verified fix that takes only two days, continuing is rational based on future prospects, not past hours. The fallacy occurs only if the decision to continue is driven by the desire to 'justify' the past 600 hours rather than an objective assessment of the remaining work.

assessment.identification_prompt: Alex claims that switching to the Linux module would mean his last six months were 'wasted.' Does continuing with the custom kernel actually recover those six months? What factors should actually determine his next step?

rubric.description: Agrees with Alex — 'He has worked too hard to quit now; he has to finish what he started.'
Feels Alex is making a mistake but thinks it's just about being tired or stubborn, without identifying the logical error regarding time.
Recognizes he should probably switch to graduate but frames it as 'cutting losses' without explicitly noting that the past time is irrelevant to the future outcome.
Identifies that the 600 hours are gone regardless of the choice and that Alex is letting the desire to justify past effort dictate a risky future decision.

Names the sunk cost fallacy, explains that the 600 hours are irrecoverable, applies the diagnostic ('If he started today with zero hours invested, would he choose the custom kernel?'), and distinguishes between rational persistence based on new data vs. irrational persistence based on past cost.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine Alex's laptop crashed yesterday and all the code was lost. He has to start from zero today. Would he choose to rebuild the custom kernel from scratch, or start the Linux module? Why does the answer change when the 'sunk cost' is removed?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Alex feels a deep psychological pain at the thought of 'wasting' six months. Is that feeling invalid? How can he reframe the value of those six months so he doesn't feel they were wasted, even if he switches projects?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Alex is intense, sleep-deprived, and defensive. He treats his code like a child he can't abandon. He speaks rapidly, trying to convince himself as much as the player.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Alex doesn't look away from the screen. 'Don't tell me to switch. You didn't spend six months on this. If I drop it now, I'm just... I'm nothing. I have to make it work.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player helps Alex separate past effort from future viability, he takes a deep breath. 'Okay. If I started today... I'd pick the Linux module.' He backs up the code for a portfolio piece but switches the active project to ensure graduation.

scenario.context: The player enters the office of Dr. Aris Thorne, Chief of Oncology at St. Jude's Memorial. For the past eighteen months, the hospital has poured $2.4 million and countless staff hours into 'Project Aethelgard,' a proprietary immunotherapy trial for rare sarcomas. Early Phase II data shows the treatment is significantly less effective than the new industry standard, 'NexaCure,' and carries higher risks of severe autoimmune reactions. The FDA has hinted they may not approve Aethelgard without a massive, costly Phase III re-design. NexaCure is already approved and available for licensing.
scenario.text: Dr. Thorne stares at the spreadsheet, rubbing his temples. 'I know the numbers look bad compared to NexaCure. But look at what we've already spent. Two point four million dollars. Eighteen months of our best researchers' lives. If we switch to licensing NexaCure now, we admit that all of that was a waste. We'd be burning two million dollars for nothing. If we push through to Phase III, we might still prove Aethelgard works for a specific sub-genotype. We can't just throw away the investment we've already made. The hospital board will crucify me if I tell them we spent millions to learn nothing.'
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Thorne is a respected researcher whose reputation is tied to innovation. He fears the political fallout of admitting failure more than the clinical risk of continuing a flawed trial.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Thorne argues for continuing the Aethelgard trial primarily because of the resources already consumed ($2.4M, 18 months), rather than a forward-looking analysis of patient outcomes and future costs. He treats the irrecoverable past investment as a reason to incur further costs.
structure.formal_form: Agent invested Cost C in Project P. Alternative Q offers superior future outcomes. Agent reasons: 'If I choose Q, Cost C is wasted. Therefore, I must continue P to justify C.' This ignores that C is lost regardless of the choice between P and Q.
structure.why_wrong: The $2.4 million and 18 months are gone regardless of the decision. Continuing the trial incurs new costs (Phase III expenses, patient risk) for a lower probability of success compared to licensing NexaCure. The decision should be based solely on future efficacy, safety, and cost, not past expenditure.
structure.counterpoint: It is not a fallacy to continue if there is genuine new evidence that Aethelgard will succeed where it previously failed, or if the specific sub-genotype hypothesis is strong enough to warrant investment on its own merits. The fallacy lies in using the *past spend* as the primary justification, rather than the *future potential*.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Thorne lists several reasons to continue the Aethelgard trial. Which of his arguments rely on resources that can never be recovered, and how does this distort his view of the best path forward for the patients?

rubric.description: Agrees with Dr. Thorne — 'He can't waste millions of dollars; he has to see it through.'
Senses Dr. Thorne is making a mistake due to pride or fear but cannot identify the specific logical error regarding the money.
Recognizes that switching to NexaCure is better practically but frames it as 'cutting losses' without explaining why the past loss is irrelevant to the future decision.
Identifies that the $2.4M is a sunk cost and explicitly states that the decision should depend only on future patient outcomes and future costs, not past spending.

Names the sunk cost fallacy, explains that the money is gone regardless of the choice, applies the 'zero-based thinking' test (would we start this trial today if we hadn't already?), and distinguishes between rational persistence based on new data vs. irrational persistence based on past spend.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the hospital received a donation of $2.4 million today specifically for cancer research, but they had no prior history with Aethelgard. Would Dr. Thorne choose to spend that new money starting the Aethelgard trial from scratch, or would he license NexaCure? Why does the answer change when the money is already gone?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Dr. Thorne worries about the 'waste' of the last 18 months. While economically irrational to let this drive the decision, is there a psychological or political reality to his fear? How can a leader acknowledge the waste without letting it dictate a bad future choice?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Thorne is intense, defensive, and visibly exhausted. He clutches a pen like a weapon and avoids eye contact when discussing the budget, focusing instead on the 'potential' of the science to mask the financial reality.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dr. Thorne doesn't offer a seat. 'If you're here to suggest we license NexaCure, don't. You think I don't see the data? But you aren't the one who has to explain to the board why we torched two million dollars on a dead end. We are this close to a breakthrough.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player successfully reframes the decision around future patient safety and the 'zero-based' question, Thorne slumps, realizing his ego is risking lives. He agrees to halt the trial, pivot to licensing NexaCure, and repurposes the Aethelgard data for a retrospective study to salvage some scientific value.

scenario.context: The varsity basketball team is preparing for the regional finals. Head Coach Miller has spent the last six months developing a complex, high-tempo offensive system called 'The Velocity.' Despite extensive practice, the team has lost four of their last five games using it, and players report confusion and fatigue. An assistant coach suggests reverting to the team's simpler, proven 'Triangle' offense which led them to the state semifinals last year.
scenario.text: Coach Miller slams his clipboard onto the bench, glaring at the stats sheet. 'I don't want to hear about switching back to the Triangle. We have spent half the season drilling Velocity. We've burned through hundreds of practice hours installing those specific cuts and screens. If we change now, all that time is wasted. The players just need to execute better. We stick with Velocity because we've already invested so much in it. Quitting now would mean those six months meant nothing.'
scenario.speaker_context: Coach Miller is a disciplined but rigid leader who prides himself on innovation and consistency, feeling personally responsible for the new system's success.

structure.pattern_description: Coach Miller argues that the team must continue using the failing 'Velocity' offense specifically because of the time and effort already invested (six months, hundreds of hours). He treats these past costs as a reason to persist, ignoring that the time is gone regardless of the choice, and that the alternative offers a higher probability of winning.
structure.formal_form: Agent invested cost C (time/effort) in failing strategy P. Superior alternative Q exists. Agent reasons: 'Because I already spent C on P, I must continue P.' But C is irrecoverable regardless of whether P or Q is chosen.
structure.why_wrong: The six months of practice are gone whether the team switches strategies or not. Continuing with a losing strategy solely to justify past investment guarantees further losses (games), whereas switching to a proven strategy maximizes future success potential.
structure.counterpoint: Persisting with a strategy can be rational if the team is on the verge of mastering it and the remaining learning curve is short. However, the fallacy occurs when the decision is driven by the desire to not 'waste' the past rather than an objective assessment of future game outcomes.

assessment.identification_prompt: Coach Miller gives a specific reason for refusing to change the offense. What is that reason, and does it logically support the idea that 'Velocity' will win the next game?

rubric.description: Agrees with the Coach – 'He's right, they can't waste all that practice time.'
Feels the Coach is being stubborn but cannot explain why the reasoning is flawed.
Suggests switching strategies is better for winning but doesn't explicitly identify the error in the Coach's logic regarding past time.
Identifies that the time already spent is irrelevant to the current decision and that the Coach is letting sunk costs dictate the strategy.

Names the sunk cost fallacy, explains that practice time is irrecoverable, applies the diagnostic ('If we hadn't practiced Velocity at all, would we start it today?'), and notes that switching minimizes future losses.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine the team woke up today with no memory of the last six months of practice. They know 'Velocity' loses games and 'Triangle' wins them. Which playbook would Coach Miller pick then?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Coach Miller says changing means the last six months were 'for nothing.' In what way is he emotionally correct, even if he is logically wrong? Why does admitting a strategy failed feel like admitting the time spent was wasted?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Coach Miller is intense, defensive about his methods, and equates changing the plan with weakness. He constantly checks his watch and gestures at the whiteboard covered in complex diagrams.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Miller crosses his arms, blocking the view of the whiteboard. 'You think I don't know we're losing? But we've put six months into this system. Six months! You don't just throw that away because of a bad streak. We run Velocity, or those hours were a lie.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player convinces Miller to look forward rather than backward, he sighs, erases the board, and says, 'Fine. If we started today, we'd run the Triangle. Let's run the Triangle.' The team regains confidence and focuses on execution rather than confusion.

scenario.context: The player attends a closed-door strategy session in the Capitol. Senator Elena Vance has championed the 'National Secure Identity Grid' (NSIG) for four years. The project has already consumed $12 billion of the federal budget, yet pilot programs in three major cities have failed due to privacy lawsuits and technical incompatibility with existing state databases. A bipartisan coalition is proposing a pivot to a decentralized, blockchain-based verification system that is cheaper, faster to deploy, and legally safer, but it would require abandoning the NSIG infrastructure entirely.
scenario.text: Vance slams her hand on the table, scattering briefing papers. 'You think I don't know the polls are bad? You think I haven't heard the critics?' She points a shaking finger at the budget projection on the screen. 'We have spent twelve billion dollars. Twelve billion! If we switch to this... this decentralized experiment now, we are admitting that money was burned. It signals weakness to our adversaries and incompetence to our voters. We are six months away from the full rollout in the Midwest. If we push through the resistance, fix the API glitches, and absorb the legal costs, the system works. We cannot let twelve billion dollars vanish into thin air just because the path got rocky. We owe it to the taxpayers to finish what we started.'
scenario.speaker_context: Senator Elena Vance, a senior Appropriations Committee member, has staked her legacy and re-election campaign on the success of the NSIG. She fears that abandoning the project will be framed as a massive waste of public funds.

structure.pattern_description: Senator Vance argues for continuing the failing NSIG project primarily because of the $12 billion already spent. She treats the past expenditure as a loss that can only be avoided by future success, ignoring that the money is gone regardless of the decision. Her reasoning conflates 'finishing what we started' with fiscal responsibility, when true responsibility requires minimizing future losses.
structure.formal_form: Agent invested resource R (money/political capital) in Project P. Project P is failing; Alternative Q offers better outcomes at lower future cost. Agent argues: 'Abandoning P makes R a total loss; continuing P justifies R.' Therefore, Agent chooses P. Error: R is irrecoverable; the choice should depend solely on future costs/benefits of P vs Q.
structure.why_wrong: The $12 billion is a sunk cost; it cannot be recovered whether the project continues or stops. Continuing the project incurs additional costs (legal fees, technical fixes, political capital) for a system that is fundamentally flawed. The decision to pivot should be based on whether the decentralized system offers better value moving forward, not on preserving the illusion that the past spending was wise.
structure.counterpoint: There is a nuance here: abandoning a massive government project does carry a real 'signaling cost' (loss of credibility) that a private company might not face. If the political damage of admitting failure is catastrophic for the party's broader agenda, continuing might be a strategic calculation rather than a pure fallacy. However, Vance's argument focuses on the money itself ('twelve billion dollars vanish'), which remains a fallacious reason regardless of political signaling.
